entries.title: Dear Abby: Holidays bring up issues of gratitude
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My sister-in-law lives across the country. For years, we shipped each other's children Christmas gifts. A few years ago, she went through a difficult divorce and has since stopped sending gifts. While we didn't discuss it, I figured it was a financial strain, which is understandable.</p><p>My issue is that we continued to send her children gifts but have never received a thank-you or even an acknowledgment. I feel it's rude, but my husband doesn't think it's a big deal. Am I wrong in feeling this way? — <i>LOVES CHRISTMAS IN CHICAGO</i></p><p><b>DEAR LOVES CHRISTMAS:</b> You are not wrong; your husband is. Those children should have been taught from an early age that it is important to acknowledge gifts they receive with a thank-you note or, at the very least, a phone call, text or email. Not to do that is, indeed, rude, but don't blame the kids. The blame falls on the parents who failed to teach them basic good manners.</p><p>Speaking of the parents, ask your sister-in-law if she is still comfortable with the gifts you send to her children. Her family's failure to show gratitude may be a hint that they feel guilty about being unable to reciprocate.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been a divorced woman for the past 10 years and am at retirement age. In the divorce, I received my house, which is almost paid for. My family, including my daughter (40), her husband (42), my son (36), my nephew (42) and my granddaughter (12), all live in that house. I moved out and into a place with a friend whose house is paid for. The adults are all employed full time. The plan was for them to pay me rent until my granddaughter graduates from high school (six more years).</p><p>Unfortunately, the only ones paying rent regularly are my son (who pays all the utilities) and my nephew, who was just diagnosed with end-stage renal disease and is going on dialysis. I have already sat down with the others and had the talk that the rent is due on the first of the month; after that, it is late. I even send them text reminders a week before it's due.</p><p>What other options do I have to get my daughter and son-in-law to pay their share of the rent? This money is supposed to be going into my retirement fund so I can retire when I'm 70 or 72. The house is in a top school district, so I don't want to evict them and jeopardize my granddaughter's education. — <i>GRANDMA LANDLADY</i></p><p><b>DEAR LANDLADY:</b> Would it be possible to enlist your son and nephew to apply some social pressure on the deadbeat couple? It would have been better if you'd had more than a verbal agreement from the start, but it's not too late. Draft a formal lease contract, including penalties for late payment, and insist that everyone sign it. If possible, have them set up a direct monthly transfer of funds from their bank accounts to yours. Always be firm and professional, and consult a lawyer if you need ideas other than eviction to encourage prompt payment.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

far. Evelyn asks Banna to define “woke.” The usually articulate group leader immediately starts hesitating. “It’s rooted in, uh, Marxism.” That’s the coherent part. Evelyn sits quietly, with Neff investing the silence with the appropriate air of triumph.</p><p>Wait! No knockdown drag-out brawl? No cogent debate? class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Relatively recently, we’ve seen far funnier and more penetrating work in a similar social-satirical vein about schooling. “The Thanksgiving Play” (also produced by Steppenwolf in the same in-the-round Ensemble Theater space as “Adirondack Chair Circle”) dealt sharply with the absurdities of trying to tell a more truthful American history in a children’s play. “Eureka Day,” produced by TimeLine Theatre in partnership with Broadway in Chicago, followed the implosion of a school board over a mandatory vaccination policy.</p><p>These plays found a way to put different viewpoints at odds with each other to mine for caustic commentary about our inability to get along. We knew where the playwrights stood in those cases, too, but we had a real sense they were willing to challenge both themselves and the audience.</p><p>And in terms of craft, those plays were also far more dramatic in their storytelling. Throughout “Adirondack Chair Circle,” there’s the sense that the most interesting characters are barely heard from, such as Banna’s nonbinary child and the school board members under pressure from multiple angles. The aforementioned stories led towards decisions the central characters themselves needed to make, but that’s not the case here.</p><p>In other words, one problem with “Adirondack Chair Circle” is that even the winning, and the losing, feels anti-climactic.</p>

entries.title: Three parents of CPS graduates face off in South Side District 10b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 10b neighborhoods: South Deering, Hegewisch, Riverdale, East Side, Chatham, South Chicago, Pullman, Calumet Heights, Avalon Park, Burnside, South Shore 

At first glance, the candidates vying to represent Chicago’s Southeast Side seem like two moms and a dad with grown children who went through Chicago Public Schools and now want to make it better for the next generation.

But under the surface are bigger political fights between the mayor and an adversary.

Connie Anderson, a paralegal and mom of twins who attend CPS, got a leg up when Mayor Brandon Johnson appointed her to fill the vacant seat in July after she filed her paperwork to run in June.

Patrick Watson works as the lead legislative aide in the office of 9th Ward Ald. Anthony Beale, one of Johnson’s harshest critics.

Then there’s write-in candidate Rosita Chatonda, a former teacher who spent years challenging her CPS firing that landed her on the district’s “do not hire” list.

With 58 schools and 21,844 students enrolled, this school board electoral district has the second-most public schools and students. Two-thirds of its students are Black and 31% are Latino.

Only 7% of the schools in the area are considered exemplary — the state’s highest rating — and 29% received the lowest designation, which is comprehensive, according to 2026 data.

Watson said Anderson’s recent appointment is “indicative of the games being played.” She has the endorsement of the Chicago Teachers Union, which is closely aligned with the mayor. He is endorsed by the Common Ground Collective, a political action committee that is anti-CTU and heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks.

“I just don't think politics belongs in education,” Watson said. “I think education belongs in education.”

Among Watson’s largest campaign donors are groups that support school choice and charter schools — the political action committee of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center. Anderson’s largest donations come from the CTU PAC and the CTU-affiliated Our Schools PAC. Chatonda has no donations on file.

The three candidates disagree on the Illinois Quantum & Microelectronics Park, the massive research and technology facility being built in their district. Anderson doubts it will have a positive impact on schools, citing pushback over a contractual agreement.

But Chatonda sees possibilities and Watson said it is “an excellent opportunity for CPS.”

entries.title: Illinois voters hit the polls with congressional power in the air on Election Day
entries.summary: <p>Tuesday’s monumental midterm elections will help determine control of Congress and serve as a litmus test of President Donald Trump’s far-reaching second term.</p><p>The results also will help determine the trajectory of his final two years in office, with Democrats potentially regaining the ability to block or at least stall the president’s agenda.</p><p>And voters in Illinois will weigh in on the first general election since Operation Midway Blitz targeted minority communities on the streets of Chicago and surrounding suburbs.</p><p>While reliably blue Illinois isn’t likely to shape the national picture, voters are weighing in on Gov. JB Pritzker’s bid for a third term and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton’s fight for Sen. Dick Durbin’s seat, which hasn’t been open since 1996. The election marks the culmination of a generational shift in Illinois politics that began with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/senator-dick-durbin-reelection" target="_blank" ><u>Durbin’s retirement announcement in April 2025.</u></a></p><p>Stratton, who faces former Illinois Republican Party chair Don Tracy, will make history if she wins the Senate seat — becoming the state’s second Black senator and the sixth Black woman to serve in the U.S. Senate.</p><p>Durbin wasn’t the only longtime member of Congress on the way out. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/30/danny-davis-wont-seek-reelection-congress" target="_blank" ><u>U.S. Reps. Danny Davis</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/05/05/rep-jan-schakowsky-announces-she-wont-seek-re-election-to-congress" target="_blank" ><u>Jan Schakowsky</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/03/jesus-chuy-garcia-reelection-dropping-out-chief-of-staff-running" target="_blank" ><u>Jesus “Chuy” Garcia</u></a> also announced their retirements.</p><p>That means Illinois’ congressional delegation is also entering a new phase, with five new members of Congress joining the fray.</p><p>Dozens of Illinois General Assembly races will determine just how strong a grasp Democrats will retain over Springfield. Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch is out to expand his caucus’ 78-40 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/16/illinois-house-district-97-election-shanahan-heitman-benton-sexual-harassment-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>super majority</u></a> — but has no guarantee of holding onto the gavel next year amid questions over his handling of a sexual harassment investigation.</p><p>And in Chicago, city voters have their first opportunity to seat a fully elected <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Board of Education</u></a>. The three-way race for board president among former principal Jessica Biggs, former teacher Hilario Dominguez and attorney Victor Henderson has drawn millions of dollars in outside spending seeking to influence leadership of the district.</p><p>The end of the midterm races will also jump-start a new clock as Democrats, including Pritzker, weigh whether to jump into the 2028 presidential fray. The Democratic governor, who has spent more than $90 million on his latest gubernatorial bid, will also have to face repeated questions about whether he’ll serve a full third term.</p><h3><b>Final pitches</b></h3><p>Pritzker, vying to become the first Illinois Democrat elected to a third term, spent the final day of the campaign before Election Day on a series of downstate get-out-the-vote events, appearing with Sens. Tammy Duckworth, Dick Durbin and Durbin’s endorsed successor, Stratton.</p><p>That followed a busy weekend of Chicago campaign events for the incumbent, who rallied with SEIU leaders who endorsed him Saturday, taking as many shots at his Republican challenger, Darren Bailey, as at his national nemesis, President Trump.</p><p>“Darren Bailey wants to undo all the progress that we've made,” Pritzker said. “He opposes raising the minimum wage. He opposes giving you benefits. He doesn't support workers' rights, and he says he wants to roll out the red carpet for Donald Trump in Illinois. … We can't let him anywhere near the governor's office.”</p><p> Bailey had a lower-key final weekend of campaigning, meeting with supporters and attending a religious service in Chicago Saturday; spending time with family and taking media interviews from his southern Illinois home entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Special interests dominate race for District 6a Downtown and on Near North Side in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 6a neighborhoods: Near North Side, West Town

This race pits a former lobbyist who leads a statewide advocacy organization with an incumbent advantage against two challengers — a special education classroom assistant backed by pro-school choice and anti-CTU groups and another who is an education researcher and consultant whose campaign is operating more independently.

Anusha Thotakura was appointed by the mayor in 2024 after coming in second among three candidates in the first school board election and is hoping to keep her seat with support from the Chicago Teachers Union and the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support workers.

Isaiah White, a school support worker, is running with thousands of dollars from The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. He also is endorsed by an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Brenda Lee Anderson, a Northwestern University lecturer on leave, is not backed by major special interest groups.

Given its location as part of the commercial and business center of the city, District 6a has just 14 public schools — the fewest of any school board electoral districts — and none are neighborhood high schools. The students who attend Chicago Public Schools here include a more diverse mix than in most districts, but the schools have more white and Asian American students than CPS as a whole.

Two of the schools in the district have the highest rating given by the state; while 60% had the lowest two distinctions, “developing” and “comprehensive,” according to 2026 state data released last week. There are now six levels of designations, up from the five up last year when the bottom two were called “comprehensive” and “intensive.”

Thotakura’s and White’s main priorities are to boost reading and math scores. Anderson’s main goal is to fix CPS’ chronic budget crisis.
entries.author: Sarah Karp

entries.title: Two newcomers race to represent South Side’s District 6b amid enrollment declines in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 6b neighborhoods: Greater Grand Crossing, Grand Boulevard, Washington Park, Near South Side, the Loop, Douglas, Woodlawn, Englewood, Fuller Park, Hyde Park

Michael Neal, a South Side native and longtime pastor, is facing off against Brittany Kimble, a lawyer and Chicago Public mom, to represent a district that stretches from the wealthy Lakeshore East neighborhood downtown through the South Loop and Greater Grand Crossing.

The two newcomer candidates are running in one of two school board races where no candidate has been endorsed by the district’s major labor unions, Chicago Teachers Union or the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support staff.

District 6b includes 37 schools and has experienced some of the city’s biggest enrollment declines, while others closer to downtown have enrolled more students over the past decade. A little over half of kids in the district attend CPS schools, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat Chicago.

Black students are overrepresented (88%) compared to District 6b’s overall Black population (64%). Meanwhile, white families are underrepresented. Less than 1% of the student population is white in a school board district that is 20% white. Families’ concerns range from wanting quality, well-resourced public schools in all neighborhoods to feeling welcome on their children’s campuses, according to the candidates.

Neal was born and raised on the South Side and graduated from CPS and now runs a nonprofit. Kimble grew up in towns throughout Illinois and now sends her daughter to a CPS school.

Improving reading and math proficiency and fixing CPS’ budget are Kimble’s top priorities. Neal wants to improve early childhood education.

The candidates are either endorsed by or have received financial support from groups that are often at odds with the Chicago Teachers Union and the mayor’s office.

Neal was endorsed by Common Ground Collective, a new anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” Neal has not reported any campaign donations.

Kimble’s campaign is endorsed by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and has received some contributions, though she insists the group has asked nothing of her. She also has received a contribution from the political action committee affiliated with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools.
entries.author: Layna Hong

entries.title: Protecting immigrant communities top priorities for District 7a candidates on the Southwest Side in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 7a neighborhoods: South Lawndale, Near West Side, Lower West Side, Garfield Ridge, Archer Heights

In this majority-Latino district, a longtime pastor and activist who fought overcrowded schools in Pilsen and was appointed to the school board by the mayor in 2024, is facing a younger challenger and Chicago Public Schools graduate who worked for a nonprofit after-school program for the past six years.

Incumbent board member Emma Lozano is endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, while Jesus Ayala Jr. has the backing of charter school advocates, groups that oppose the CTU and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council — which represents thousands of support staff in CPS and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Ayala tried to run in 2024, but his name was removed from the ballot after a successful challenge to the signatures on his nomination paperwork.

This Southwest Side district is home to 48 public schools. Last year, 64% received the state’s second-highest designation, “commendable,” while 4.5% received an “intensive” designation, indicating they remained among the bottom 5% of low-income schools in the state for four years after receiving comprehensive support or continued to have a graduation rate of 67% or below.

The students who attend District 7a schools are primarily Latino, matching the community demographics, and most come from families with low incomes. Nearly half are English learners.

Both Lozano and Ayala identified protecting immigrant communities and securing progressive revenue among their priorities, but they want to take different paths to get there.

For example, Lozano voted to pass a Chicago Public Schools budget that assumed additional revenue from the state. Ayala said relying on unsecured funds is a mistake. These differences have led to dueling endorsements in the race from the CTU and SEIU, labor unions that were once close allies but are now fighting for influence on the school board.

Ayala has outraised Lozano, drawing his largest campaign donations from the political action committees of SEIU and the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. Lozano’s biggest donations have come from Our Schools PAC, a CTU-affiliated PAC.
entries.author: Emmanuel Camarillo

entries.title: Two latina candidates in Southwest Side’s District 7b aim to improve special education, protect immigrants
entries.summary:
District 7b neighborhoods: Brighton Park, Lower West Side, Archer Heights, Bridgeport, Gage Park, West Elsdon, Armour Square, McKinley Park

Two Latinas with backgrounds in public service are vying to represent a slice of the Southwest Side that has one of the highest shares of schools in Chicago Public Schools with the state’s top two performance designations.

Incumbent Yesenia Lopez was elected to the school board in 2024 with the backing of the Chicago Teachers Union. Without the CTU’s backing this time, she faces a challenge from Erika Diaz-Chavez, a project manager at the Chicago Park District who attended private schools growing up. Diaz-Chavez’s biggest campaign donation has come from the Illinois Network of Charter Schools’ political arm. The Urban Center, which promotes school choice and private schools, has also contributed to her campaign.

Lopez is endorsed and backed financially by the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents thousands of CPS support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. She is also endorsed by Our Schools Chicago. That group’s views are aligned with the CTU and has endorsed all the same candidates plus Lopez.

There are 34 schools in District 7b, 13% of which ranked among the top 10% in Illinois last year. A majority of the schools — 73% — received the second-highest designation, “commendable,” and 13% of the schools were designated as “targeted,” meaning that one or more student groups are at or below the level of all students in the lowest-performing 5% of schools.

District 7b schools serve the highest percentage of Hispanic students in CPS, but a few schools also serve predominantly Asian American students. About 84% of students come from families with low incomes, and around half are English learners.

Both candidates say they want to provide more special education resources for students in response to parents’ concerns. They also want to ensure CPS is doing enough to protect immigrant families amid increased immigration enforcement in the city.

But their views diverge on Sustainable Community Schools, a program favored by the CTU that gives dozens of schools additional funds to partner with community organizations and provide extra services for families.

Diaz-Chavez isn’t sure the model is delivering results and wants to evaluate the program before spending more money on it. Lopez sees the model as a boon to families and supports it, though she agrees the district should track its progress.
entries.author: Elvia Malagón

entries.title: Far Southwest Side’s Angel Gutierrez is headed for re-election to represent District 8a in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 8a neighborhoods: Ashburn, Garfield Ridge, Clearing, West Lawn, Chicago Lawn, West Elsdon

With full campaign coffers and support from deep-pocketed groups that support school choice, incumbent school board member Angel Gutierrez is guaranteed to keep his seat after nobody filed paperwork to run against him.

Gutierrez, a nonprofit leader and Garfield Ridge resident, is running unopposed to represent this district on the Far Southwest Side where 60% of the population is Hispanic — roughly double the city’s overall percentage. Likewise, across the 29 schools in this district, the majority of students, 77%, are Hispanic.

Overall, students in this district are more likely to attend their neighborhood schools than in other communities. For elementary school, 69% of students attend their neighborhood schools compared to 56% citywide. For high school, 28% of students in District 8a choose a local school, compared to 23% citywide, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat.

The area has leaned more conservative than other parts of the city and is home to more families than single-person households. In 2023, voters here heavily favored mayoral candidate Paul Vallas, a former Chicago Public Schools CEO, over Mayor Brandon Johnson, a former Chicago Teachers Union organizer. In 2024, most precincts favored Donald Trump for president.

Gutierrez wants to improve special education, increase opportunities to learn skilled trades, and ensure access to reliable transportation, including school buses — proposals he said would benefit students attending their neighborhood schools.

Gutierrez supports continuing CPS’ strategy of allowing families to choose from a range of schools outside their neighborhood. He is endorsed by groups that support school choice, charter schools and oppose the Chicago Teachers Union. He also is endorsed by the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. The political action committees of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and SEIU and other supporters have donated to Gutierrez’ campaign even though he is running uncontested.

He is also the only board member calling for the state to opt into the Trump administration’s federal tax-credit scholarship program, which offers a tax credit for donations made to organizations that grant scholarships for students to attend private schools or to pay for other education needs. Illinois has not agreed to participate.

Gutierrez sends his children to a Catholic school.
entries.author: Layna Hong

entries.title: College student challenges police detective in race for District 8b, South Side and Southwest Side in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 8b neighborhoods: New City, Chicago Lawn, Gage Park, McKinley Park, Bridgeport, the Loop, Brighton Park, West Lawn, Near South Side, Armour Square

Juan Ignacio González, a veteran Chicago Police detective and local coffee shop owner, is running against college student Alexander Angeles to represent District 8b, a long, narrow swath that stretches across the Southwest Side.

Angeles joined the race as a write-in candidate at the end of August. Earlier this summer, the Chicago election authority kicked incumbent and Mayor Brandon Johnson appointee Cydney Wallace off the ballot due to challenges to her petition signatures.

González, a Back of the Yards resident, said he was motivated to run for school board in the mostly Latino district after hearing from parents who were concerned about students being used as “political pawns” on May Day. The Chicago Teachers Union and Chicago Public Schools reached an agreement to keep schools open on May 1 while allowing civic actions after some back-and-forth over whether to call off school for demonstrations.

“Parents were speaking about some of the challenges and low academic standards we’re facing … and those are issues that I agree with,” he said. “I feel like in my community, there’s no voice for individuals that oftentimes cannot vote or aren’t part of the political system. I was asked to consider it, I looked at the layout, and felt I can help kids in the community.”

A recent graduate of Hancock College Prep High School and University of Illinois Chicago political science major, Angeles said he is running to be a voice for students, a trait he believes is lacking among board members.

Gonzalez is backed by groups that support school choice and oppose the Chicago Teachers Union. His two largest campaign contributions come from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, which says its mission is to “give voice to a centrist community in Chicago.” Angeles had no donations on file as of last week.

There are nearly 25,000 school-aged children in District 8b and nearly three-quarters attend a Chicago public school, according to CPS data compiled by Chalkbeat. Matching citywide averages, about 59% of students choose neighborhood elementary schools, while 22% choose neighborhood high schools.

The students enrolled here are primarily Latino, at 68%, while about 19% are Black and 7% are white.

None of District 8b’s schools received the state’s “exemplary” top rating last year, but 70% ranked at the second-best “commendable” level. Some 9% of the schools received the state’s lowest designation, “intensive,” indicating they remained among the bottom 5% of low-income schools in the state for four years after receiving comprehensive support or continued to have a graduation rate of 67% or below.
entries.author: Kate Grossman

entries.title: Far Southwest Side pits a school psychologist against a speech-language pathologist in District 9b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 9b neighborhoods: Roseland, West Pullman, Morgan Park, Beverly, Mount Greenwood, Washington Heights 

Two candidates — a retired Chicago Public Schools psychologist currently on the school board and a former CPS mom and speech-language pathologist — are running to represent the far South Side, an area with 46 public schools, most of which are neighborhood schools, with few privately run charters and lottery-based magnets.

Incumbent Therese Boyle spent 35 years working for the district, while challenger Katherine Dunneback is currently an adjunct clinical professor at Saint Xavier University. Boyle is endorsed by groups that oppose the teachers union and support school choice, and she is also backed by the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Dunneback is endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union.

Enrollment is an issue across much of the district, with just 13% of CPS students choosing to attend their zoned public high schools, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat. Nearly 57% chose their local elementary school. The majority of students in this school board district are Black, while 10% are Hispanic and 11% are white. The majority of schools in the area were designated last year as “commendable,” the state’s second highest ranking.

Both Dunneback and Boyle had children attend Chicago Public Schools for a time before going to private schools. Dunneback’s children attended a Morgan Park neighborhood elementary school. Boyle said one of her daughters attended a Beverly public school for preschool.

Boyle said residents are focused on making sure the district is “spending money wisely,” while Dunneback said her neighbors are concerned about school overcrowding and closures.

The two candidates agree on academics, including imposing strict limits on AI and electronic devices, but disagree on charter schools and school closures. Boyle favors charter schools and school consolidation when equitable and cost effective. Dunneback opposes charter schools and spoke of expanding a CPS and CTU program that turns neighborhood schools into community hubs as an alternative to closures.

Neither candidate wants to raise property taxes to the maximum to fund schools, according to our CPS School Board questionnaire. But Dunneback says board members should work with other elected officials to fund schools through other tax policies, whereas Boyle says CPS is not spending wisely.

Boyle has received contributions from the SEIU IL Council political action committee and the Common Ground Collective, a PAC that is anti-CTU and heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks. Dunneback’s top contributions are from the CTU-affiliated Our Schools PAC and CTU PAC.
entries.author: Kristen Schorsch

entries.title: Grammy Award-winning hip-hop artist faces CTU backed write-in candidate for South Side District 10a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 10a neighborhoods: South Shore, Woodlawn, Greater Grand Crossing, Hyde Park, Kenwood, South Chicago, Douglas, Oakland 

When Che “Rhymefest” Smith won a seat on the school board two years ago, he proudly wore the moniker of an independent after triumphing over candidates with support from the Chicago Teachers Union and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools.

“I will tell you that my connections in the community got me here, my work got me here,” said the Grammy Award-winning hip-hop artist turned activist and politician. “Money didn't get me here.”

This time is different. Smith will be the lone name on the ballot to represent District 10a.

Stretching from Bronzeville to South Shore, the district’s 33 schools include some of the South Side’s most sought-after schools, including Kenwood Academy High School and Murray Language Academy Elementary School, as well as several neighborhood schools that are considered low-performing and have lost enrollment in recent years. A large percentage of students are choosing neighborhood high schools, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat. More than 88% of the students in 10a are Black and nearly 7% are Hispanic.

Unlike in 2024, Smith is now a known entity who has consistently voted against items pushed by the CTU and, for that, has received endorsements and donations from groups that oppose the union. Still, Smith says he would welcome the union’s support and counsel.

He’s raised more than $100,000 in campaign donations, even though his only opponent, nonprofit leader Tameka Walton, is running as a write-in candidate after her name was booted off the ballot.

Walton said she represents two important constituencies that Smith doesn’t. One, she’s a mom who had to advocate to get her children into CPS schools where they could thrive. She is also the executive director and founder of a nonprofit that works in schools with children who have experienced trauma.

“I’m looking beyond how much trouble it was for me to navigate (CPS), but I’m also looking at, as a parent, the things that I want to see done,” she said. “The school should be a safe and welcoming space for both the students and the parents.

Walton picked up the CTU’s endorsement and has received donations from the CTU PAC and the CTU-affiliated Our Schools PAC.
entries.author: Kristen Schorsch

entries.title: Retired police officer and community advocate face off in Far NW Side District 1a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 1a neighborhoods: O’Hare, Norwood Park, Forest Glen, Jefferson Park, Dunning, Edison Park

A retired Chicago police officer allied with two local aldermen is looking to unseat a longtime community development advocate who gained an incumbent advantage when the mayor appointed him to represent this district on Chicago’s Far Northwest Side.

Ed Bannon is hoping to fend off Margie Luczak’s challenge with support from the Chicago Teachers Union and the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support staff. But Luczak has secured the backing of special interest groups that favor school choice and charter schools.

Although the school board elections are nonpartisan, political undercurrents are present in voters’ decisions about which candidate aligns with their values. On the Far Northwest Side, voters have been more receptive to conservative candidates than much of Chicago and could be more sympathetic to an “anti-establishment” platform.

It’s one of the few areas in Chicago that leaned toward President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. And in 2023, many voters here picked former CPS CEO Paul Vallas over Mayor Brandon Johnson.

But the race is inherently much narrower in its scope of issues than a Congressional or presidential campaign, which could reveal diverging attitudes specifically on the topic of education.

This Far Northwest Side district is home to 22 schools that enroll more white students than Chicago Public Schools as a whole, but are more diverse than the voting population. Families here choose their neighborhood public schools at the highest rate in the city — a whopping 75% compared to a citywide average of about 46%.

Although Bannon was appointed by Johnson, he hasn’t always aligned with him, most notably when he voted last year in favor of the CPS budget plan Johnson’s other appointees were trying to block. Bannon’s record has earned him endorsements from the Chicago Teachers Union and SEIU Illinois State Council.

Voters looking for a change in leadership may opt for Luczak, who served on Chicago’s police force for more than 25 years. In many ways, her campaign represents a foil to Bannon’s union-backed candidacy.

She proudly says she’s not a “CTU puppet” and is supported by contributions from the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, an organization that advocates for centrist leadership and school choice, including private schools. But she has little direct experience in education.
entries.author: Lauren FitzPatrick

entries.title: Outside groups are spending heavily on Far NW Side District 1b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 1b neighborhoods: Portage Park, Dunning, Irving Park, Belmont Cragin, North Park, Montclare, Albany Park

The two women vying to represent Chicago’s Northwest Side are no strangers to politics — one ran for school board in 2024 and the other has run campaigns or worked for other elected officials for more than 15 years.

Michelle Pierre lost by a thin margin in 2024, which was her first time running for office after spending more than 25 years working in education as a teacher, principal in public and charter schools, district administrator and leadership coach. Claudia Peralta is making her debut as a candidate, but has worked with multiple politicians on the Northwest Side, including U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez.

District 1b is home to 20 Chicago public schools, which is among the fewest of all the school board voting districts. Families here choose their neighborhood elementary schools at a higher rate than in other parts of the city — but not their high schools. Students who attend school in this district are mostly Hispanic — 69% — while 19% are white and 5% are Black, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat.

This matchup isn’t so much about individual policies as it is about differing strategies for how to govern as a Chicago school board member.

Pierre is metrics-driven, weighing district financial decisions against their return on investment for students bettering their academic outcomes. Peralta is rooted in political savvy and using government relationships to secure the resources Chicago Public Schools needs for students to thrive. District 1b voters will ultimately choose which style they want to see prioritized.

Outside groups are spending heavily on this race. As of last week, it had attracted more spending by political action committees and super PACs — more than $830,000 — than any other school board district.

More than half of that came from the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective, which has thrown money behind Pierre and against Peralta. Pierre also got funding from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, an organization that advocates for centrist leadership and school choice, including private schools.

The winner will replace Jennifer Custer, who has served the past two years and ran for school board president before dropping out of the race in August.
entries.author: Lauren FitzPatrick

entries.title: Taxing the wealthy verses belt-tightening is at the heart of District 2a Far North Side Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 2a neighborhoods: West Ridge, Rogers Park, North Park

An attorney is challenging an incumbent with a background in community organizing in a two-way race to represent one of Chicago’s most culturally diverse areas along the Far North Side lakefront.

Elected in 2024, Ebony DeBerry favors taxing corporations and the wealthy to confront Chicago Public Schools’ budget woes. Her opponent sees belt-tightening as a path forward. Hector Morales, an attorney who attended CPS, said the district must spend more efficiently.

District 2a is home to a large number of immigrant families. More than 80 languages are spoken throughout the Rogers Park neighborhood alone, according to the Rogers Park Business Alliance.

The district’s 18 schools serve a diverse group of students too. Around 33% are Hispanic, nearly 26% are Asian American, 22% are Black and almost 15% are white, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat. CPS students in this district are more likely to choose their neighborhood schools compared to the city overall. More than 40% of high school students attend their neighborhood schools, compared with only 24% across the city.

The two candidates’ views differ on how to fund and invest in bilingual and dual-language education programs while also addressing CPS’ budget deficit.

“We have to find ways to make corporations, millionaires and billionaires pay their fair share,” DeBerry said in an interview, while Morales said board members “need to make sure we’re using what we got now, before we start asking folks for more money.”

DeBerry, a former CPS teacher, won 43% of the vote in 2024, edging out three other candidates.

DeBerry is one of four candidates who’s been endorsed by both the Chicago Teachers Union and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff. Political action committees for both unions have contributed to DeBerry’s campaign too.

Morales has been endorsed by the Common Ground Collective, a political action committee that is anti-CTU, is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Morales is also endorsed by the Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools.
entries.author: Layna Hong

entries.title: Incumbent appointed by Johnson faces challenger backed by Michael Sacks in District 2b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 2b neighborhoods: Lincoln Square, Edgewater, Albany Park, Uptown, North Park 

A retired Chicago Public Schools teacher appointed by the mayor is facing off against a former special education teacher worried about the school district’s debt burden.

Incumbent Debby Pope is endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, while Kyna Lenhof has the endorsement of the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective. A third candidate, Daniel Basco, suspended his campaign in October and endorsed Lenhof, though his name remains printed on the ballot.

District 2b is one of Chicago’s most culturally diverse areas and is home to 18 public schools. Students who attend schools in the district are 40% Hispanic, 30% white, nearly 15% Asian American and 9% Black, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat.

Though none of the schools in the district last year earned the state’s highest rating of “exemplary,” a high share, 79%, earned the state’s second-highest rating of “commendable,” data compiled by Chalkbeat shows.

And 62% of students in District 2b chose to attend their neighborhood school — the second-highest share in the city and well above CPS average of 46%.

Both candidates have touted their experience working in classrooms and listed adequate classroom funding and resources among their main priorities. But their thoughts on how to secure that vary.

Pope said she supports increasing funding for schools by taxing the rich, while Lenhof said she wants to reduce the district’s reliance on high-interest loans.

Pope was appointed to the board by Mayor Brandon Johnson in 2024 after the mass resignation of his first group of school board appointees amid tensions with former CPS CEO Pedro Martinez.

She got the nod from the powerful teachers union, while Lenhof was endorsed by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that supports charters and advocates for school choice across public and private schools. Lenhof was also endorsed by the Common Ground Collective, which is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Lenhof’s campaign has been buoyed by contributions from Common Ground and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, while much of Pope’s support has come from the CTU and groups aligned with the union, including the Chicago Working Families PAC.

Earlier this summer, Common Ground released an ad attacking Pope for voting in favor of a CPS budget plan that assumes the district will receive $150 million more in state funding than projected.

The day before the vote, Lenhof also released a statement criticizing Pope.

“Our current board member, appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson, has continually supported high-interest loans that burden taxpayers and weaken CPS’s financial future,” Lenhof wrote.
entries.author: Emmanuel Camarillo

entries.title: Tackling the budget deficit separates these two progressive candidates in the Near NW Side District 3b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 3b neighborhoods: Humboldt Park, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, West Town, Hermosa

Two men who both grew up in Humboldt Park, graduated from selective-enrollment Chicago public high schools, and became teachers through Teach for America are facing off — again — in the race to represent a district that spans from West Town to Belmont Cragin.

Both candidates identify as progressives. Incumbent board member Carlos Rivas Jr. won in 2024 with 54% of the vote. Rivas has taken a more fiscally conservative approach to the school budget than his opponent.

Rivas has support from the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS school support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years, charter school advocates, and some Northwest Side officials. He is also endorsed by the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Jason Dónes is backed by the Chicago Teachers Union and several Northwest Side elected officials.

A few days before the election, Rivas responded to the release of records that showed he was suspended from his job at a charter school in 2018 after he became intoxicated at a work event and engaged in “unwanted touching” of a co-worker.

Rivas said the incident happened at a difficult time in his life when he was caring for his dying mother and that he took responsibility for what happened and got help through an employee assistance program.

“I believe in accountability, growth and second chances,” he told the Chicago Sun-Times in a statement.

Schools in District 3b are struggling with teacher and counselor shortages, higher property taxes, and low enrollment amid rapid gentrification. The district includes a mix of 32 schools serving mostly Latino students.

Rivas and Dónes both care about protecting immigrant students from federal immigration agents, supporting more affordable housing, and securing more resources and community partnerships for CPS families. Rivas says he wants less interference from the mayor on the board and to move away from using loans that will increase CPS’ budget deficit.

Dónes, a CPS parent, is looking to increase budget transparency, push for creative solutions within the existing budget framework, and said on our questionnaire that he won’t accept contributions from corporations or “private interest groups funded by billionaires and millionaires.”

Rivas’ outside support is about five times greater than Dónes’. As of last week, more than half of the $502,000 backing Rivas came from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools while another $123,000 came from the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective. All of Dónes’ outside support comes from the CTU, totaling about $22,000.
entries.author: Lauren FitzPatrick

entries.title: Incumbent backed by CTU faces challenger funded by pro-charter forces in NW Side District 3a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 3a neighborhoods: Avondale, Irving Park, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, Hermosa, Albany Park

A newcomer building a coalition of support from private donors and charter school advocates is challenging a longtime community activist with ties to the Chicago Teachers Union and Northwest Side elected officials in the race to represent District 3a.

Incumbent Norma Rios Sierra, a Logan Square organizer appointed to the school board in 2024 by Mayor Brandon Johnson, is hoping to hold onto her seat against Peter Gonzales, a lawyer for the Illinois Secretary of State.

Schools in District 3a are struggling with teacher shortages, arts program cuts, charter school closings and access to mental health support. The Northwest Side district has a mix of 23 dual-language, charter and alternative schools serving mostly Latino students.

While both candidates have similar positions on increasing funds for CPS and supporting immigrant families, their support differs.

Rios Sierra is backed by the CTU and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents thousands of CPS support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. She’s one of only four candidates to be endorsed by both unions. SEIU’s political action committee and another PAC funded by the CTU have contributed to Rios Sierra’s campaign, too.

Gonzales has support from the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, a pro-school choice group, and the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” Gonzales is also backed by the Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools.

Gonzales advocates for equitable teacher wages that can strengthen student test scores and expand opportunities for students, such as having a stronger trades pipelines and more school choice, while Rios Sierra wants to see more mental health resources for students and more art and extracurricular programs for neighborhood schools.
entries.author: Layna Hong

entries.title: Mayor Johnson ally faces two challengers keen on addressing mounting budget deficits in North Side District 4a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 4a neighborhoods: Lakeview, Uptown, North Center, Edgewater

The race in this North Side district pits a retired educator appointed to the current school board against two challengers who say board members have faltered on fiscal responsibility and setting ambitious goals for Chicago Public Schools.

Karen Zaccor, a longtime Uptown teacher and advocate appointed by the mayor in 2024 after coming in second among six candidates, will face teacher recruitment and retention expert Ellen Sherratt and stem cell researcher Angel Alvarez.

The area along the north lakefront is home to 15 schools, less than almost any other school board district. About 57% of students attend their neighborhood elementary schools — a little higher than the 46% citywide average — but that share is much lower for high school. The district serves a diverse student body; about 35% are Hispanic, 27% are white, almost 24% are Black and nearly 8% are Asian, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat.

Zaccor has voted consistently with a majority bloc of board members appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson or elected with backing from the Chicago Teachers Union, Johnson’s former employer and close ally. Her priorities also echo those of the union, which has endorsed Zaccor. They include pushing for a billionaires tax or other progressive state revenue to boost school fundings.

Her opponents Sherratt and Alvarez argue that the district must do more to address mounting deficits than lobby the state.

Sherratt has drawn endorsements from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years, and other groups that oppose the CTU. Those include the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee.

Common Ground and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools have spent more than $600,000 on this race, bolstering Sherratt and attacking Zaccor. And Sherratt has raised more than $260,000 individually — the most of all candidates, as of Monday. Alvarez has no outside PAC support.

Sherratt said she would push for setting ambitious student achievement goals.

Alvarez, who leads a family advisory board for the district, said he would champion more responsive special education and protect families from higher property taxes.
entries.author: Lauren FitzPatrick

entries.title: Ellen Rosenfeld is running unopposed in District 4b covering Lincoln Park and parts of Lakeview in the Chicago School Board election
entries.summary:
District 4b neighborhoods: Lincoln Park, North Center, Lakeview, Logan Square

Ellen Rosenfeld, a former Chicago Public Schools teacher and district engagement specialist, is running unopposed to keep the North Side seat she won handily in 2024 against five other would-be school board members in the city’s most crowded race.

That year, pro-school choice groups spent heavily to back her and oppose a teachers union-backed candidate.

She’s made serving on the board her full-time role the past two years after leaving her position with CPS Family and Community Engagement.

Rosenfeld is part of a block of seven elected members who have opposed the mayor’s appointees and elected allies on the board, who make up a majority. She has backing from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, and other groups that oppose the Chicago Teachers Union, the mayor’s former employer and key ally. As of last week, she’d received a notable $100,000 in campaign contributions, mostly from individuals, though she’s the only candidate on the ballot.

The former Local School Council chair and mother of four CPS graduates argues the current board has been too mired in politics and susceptible to outside pressure. But she feels the incoming fully elected board could preside over an academic resurgence, from a rise in reading proficiency to a decrease in chronic absenteeism, one of her key concerns. She said the next board must rally around a set of goals for improving the district.

“Without a shared vision, it’s almost impossible to get the good stuff done,” Rosenfeld said.

District 4b is home to 18 schools, including several high-performing neighborhood schools, coveted magnets and a popular selective-enrollment high school, Lane Tech College Prep. Families here choose their neighborhood schools at higher rates than in many other school board districts.

The school board district serves a significantly higher percentage of white students than the district as a whole. About 46% of students are white, 25% are Hispanic, 12% are Black and 9% are Asian American, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat. District 4b also has the highest share of schools that received the state’s top rating of “exemplary” for academic performance last year.
entries.author: Kalyn Belsha

entries.title: Three Austin residents square off over school choice in the West Side’s District 5a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 5a neighborhoods: Austin, Humboldt Park, West Town, Montclare

A Realtor backed by school choice advocates is looking to unseat a longtime education activist with ties to the Chicago Teachers Union in this race on the city’s West Side. Also in the mix: a retired special education teacher running as a write-in candidate.

Incumbent Aaron “Jitu” Brown, a veteran community organizer, wants to secure more state funding and trim administrative overhead in Chicago Public Schools. Challenger LaPamela Williams, an Austin native who attended Lane Tech College Prep, wants to increase financial accountability and cut expenses that aren’t benefiting students. Kernetha Jones, who was removed from the ballot, wants to see test scores improve before putting more money into what she calls a “failed system.”

The district stretches from the majority-Black Austin neighborhood to the west, through sections of Garfield Park and Humboldt Park, ending with Ukrainian Village to the east. The wide swath of the West Side encompasses 39 schools serving mostly Black and Latino students. After decades of disinvestment, many schools are struggling to stabilize enrollment and bring students up to grade level.

More than half of schools in the district last year received one of the state’s two lowest academic performance ratings, the highest share in the city, indicating many schools are in need of “targeted” or “intensive” support.

Students who live in District 5a are less likely to attend their neighborhood school than students in most parts of the city, particularly for high school. Less than 7% of high schoolers in this area chose their neighborhood option, according to CPS data. One high school, Frederick Douglass Academy in Austin, had just 27 students last year, and has become a focal point in debates over how CPS should address declining enrollment.

All three candidates live in Austin. Their views diverge when it comes to independently run public charter schools, with Brown and Jones opposing their expansion, while Williams supports opening more if there is community support.

The Illinois Network of Charter Schools has endorsed and is financially backing Williams. She is also endorsed by the Urban Center and Common Ground Collective, a new political action committee funded by billionaire Michael Sacks that opposes the CTU. Browns is endorsed and financially supported by the CTU and the CTU-funded group Our Schools Chicago. Jones, the write-in candidate, did not have any major endorsements as of last week.
entries.author: Lisa Kurian Philip

entries.title: West Side’s economically diverse District 5b wrestles with declining enrollment as candidates vie for seat on Chicago School Board
entries.summary:
District 5b neighborhoods: North Lawndale, Near West Side, East Garfield Park, West Garfield Park, West Town 

The two candidates battling to represent a large swath of the West Side are taking a second stab at securing a school board seat. Incumbent school board member Michilla “Kyla” Blaise started a campaign in 2024 but withdrew at the last minute, while her challenger, Anthony Hargrove, failed to make the ballot two years ago.

Blaise, a political aide who was appointed to the school board by Mayor Brandon Johnson in 2024, is backed by the Chicago Teachers Union. Hargrove, who runs programs to help dropouts get back in school, has support from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, charter school advocates like the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, and the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that’s heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks.

District 5b is one of the school board’s most economically diverse, stretching from the wealthy West Loop to historically disinvested neighborhoods such as North Lawndale and Garfield Park. It includes several neighborhood high schools struggling with declining enrollment, as well as some of CPS’ most in-demand magnet schools. Students who attend school here are mostly Black and Hispanic.

Students in District 5b are less likely to attend their neighborhood school than students in any other voting district in the city. Only 6% chose their local high school, while 35% chose their neighborhood elementary school.

The candidates have homed in on different issues. Blaise said she is focused on increasing funding for CPS, addressing declining enrollment and improving student mental health, while Hargrove has zeroed in on improving reading and math proficiency, refining special education and expanding vocational and career education.

The two candidates align on some issues. They both support stronger restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence and cellphones in the classroom, and both oppose closing schools for any reason.

Notably, Blaise led the effort to pass a CPS budget that reversed some proposed cuts but banked on the state to provide $150 million in funding it had not committed. On his candidate questionnaire, Hargrove said the school board should continue to advocate for additional state funding and look for other savings “before cutting classroom programs or student services.”
entries.author: Elvia Malagón

entries.title: Chicago School Board Election 2026: The citywide race for president
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s first-ever race for school board president has generated millions in political contributions, political jockeying by special-interest groups and stirred controversy in a divisive and heated campaign.</p><p>On Tuesday, voters across the city will choose among three candidates to lead the Chicago Board of Education: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>. The person elected to this powerful, but unpaid position, will represent the board publicly, run the board’s monthly meetings and help set the agenda for a body that oversees a roughly $10 billion annual budget. The new leader will work with 20 other members to set a vision and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/21/what-you-need-to-know-about-chicagos-historic-school-board-election" target="_blank" ><u>goals for Chicago Public Schools for the next four years</u></a>.</p><p>Given the president’s influence, the vast majority of money flooding the school board election is focused on that race. Of the nearly <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/school-board/money/#mm-president" target="_blank" ><u>$8.3 million raised directly by the candidates</u></a>, $5.2 million has been collected in the president’s race, including by two candidates who have since withdrawn. Biggs has raised $1.8 million, Dominguez $1.7 million and Henderson about $700,000 — nearly all of that money he loaned himself.</p><p>When spending by super PACs, which can’t coordinate with candidates, is factored in, $13.9 million<b> </b>has been spent supporting or opposing candidates, according to an analysis by the Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><p>This includes $3.5 million<b> </b>to oppose Dominguez, bombarding voters with negative ads, by groups that don’t want the Chicago Teachers Union-endorsed candidate to lead the board. PACs funded by the CTU have spent just $577,000 in support of his campaign.</p><p>Outside political groups and unions — the Common Ground Collective and the SEIU — have spent another $1.8 million supporting Biggs.</p><p>Henderson has no outside money, a fact he prides himself on.</p><p>For many of those opponents, the race is seen as a test ahead of the February mayoral election, when Mayor Brandon Johnson is running for re-election. Opponents of the CTU are aiming to show they can take down the union, which currently holds the majority on the 21-member school board. Johnson remains closely allied with the union, which helped catapult their former organizer to office in 2023.</p><p>Dominguez is CTU’s former deputy political director who is on leave from the union and as a CPS special education teacher. The Chicago Public Schools graduate is running on a progressive platform and proposing big initiatives, including expanding preschool to all 3-year-olds, and he is demanding more education money from the state, rather than cutting to confront a deficit. The CTU and Our Schools, the political action committee it’s funding, are almost exclusively funding Dominguez’s campaign as the union tries to hold on to control of the school board.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-200000" name="image-200000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/25da3fe/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff1%2Ff9%2F9be8b174430ba6bcabc4054c14b5%2Fcpsprezresults-2611xx-24.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5f1d857/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff1%2Ff9%2F9be8b174430ba6bcabc4054c14b5%2Fcpsprezresults-2611xx-24.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5fa2e3b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff1%2Ff9%2F9be8b174430ba6bcabc4054c14b5%2Fcpsprezresults-2611xx-24.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Board of Education presidential candidate Hilario Dominguez, daps up Fred Hampton Jr. during a ribbon cutting for the New City Childcare and Early Learning Daycare located in the Englewood neighborhood on Nov. 2, 2026. entries.title: JB Pritzker and Darren Bailey square off again in Illinois governor race
entries.summary:
A gubernatorial rematch four years in the making comes to a head Tuesday night in Gov. JB Pritzker’s bid for a rare third term over Republican challenger Darren Bailey.

The Associated Press called their 2022 contest the minute the polls closed en route to Pritzker’s nearly 13-percentage-point reelection victory over the southern Illinois farmer and former state legislator, who needs to win over Chicago-area voters for any hope of becoming the first Republican to win a statewide office in 12 years.

Independent candidate Collin Corbett, a fiscal conservative who supports abortion rights, aims to play the role of spoiler by picking up moderate voters in a deeply polarized political environment.

Pritzker, a billionaire heir to the Hyatt hotel fortune, has used his astronomical financial advantage in the race to remind voters of the state’s 12 credit rating upgrades and a slew of progressive legislative victories he has shepherded through the General Assembly since unseating GOP former Gov. Bruce Rauner in 2018.

Pritzker’s self-funded, $90 million-plus campaign has also blanketed the internet and airwaves with ads painting Bailey as a lackey of President Donald Trump, who campaigned alongside Bailey four years ago and has endorsed him once again.

Bailey — who raised his profile in the Illinois General Assembly early in the COVID-19 pandemic as a vociferous opponent of Pritzker’s mitigation measures — has generally distanced himself from Trump this time around. The president remains unpopular with voters in Cook County and the collar counties, which served as the foundation of the Illinois GOP until Trump’s rise to power.

A staunch opponent of abortion rights, Bailey has emphasized he still wouldn’t have any power to limit protections on the procedure that have been championed by Pritzker and a deep blue legislature.

Instead, Bailey has used his limited campaign resources — about $525,000 on hand in the final week of the race — to keep the focus on the rising cost of living, education and crime.

“People are ready for change,” Bailey told the Sun-Times. “We didn't really sense that so much four years ago here in the city, but the high cost of living, the high cost of doing business seems to be taking a toll now. People are paying more attention.”

Bailey moved into a Chicago apartment after running away with the GOP primary in order to interact more with city voters. But the strategy has also drawn an election board complaint from the Democratic Party of Illinois for not reporting rent on campaign finance reports.

And while Bailey said his campaign focus was gaining ground in the vote-rich Chicago area, he and running mate Aaron Del Mar set out on a mostly downstate bus tour during the final week of the race urging Republicans to turn out to vote.

A win for Pritzker would make him the first Illinois governor elected to a third term since Republican Jim Thompson in 1982, and the first-ever Democrat to do so in Illinois.

It would also immediately beg the question of how long Pritzker’s attention will be totally devoted to the state — and whether he’ll launch a campaign for president in 2028.

Republicans have long complained the incumbent has viewed the office as a stepping stone to the White House, and Pritzker himself has hardly quelled presidential speculation.

But he maintains he has unfinished business in Springfield after two terms spanning some of the most tumultuous years in state history, from a global pandemic to a chaotic federal deportation campaign and numerous run-ins with the Trump administration throughout it all.

“I’m somebody that still believes in getting big things done,” Pritzker said. “We're on our way to having truly universal preschool in the state of Illinois. That's taken a couple of years for us to ramp up the funding for… And here we are eight years later, I think I've learned a lot about how to protect people in this state from Donald Trump and from his policies, and I'm going to continue to do that.”

Corbett, the independent, says his mostly self-funded campaign’s research suggests he’d do well in a head-to-head matchup with Pritzker, and says he backs more measured spending cuts than those proposed by Bailey.

“[Democrats] have got all the money so they can run a bunch of TV ads that say, ‘Look how fiscally responsible we are and look how we're lowering your taxes,’ even though both things aren't true,” Corbett said. “And then they go down, they govern and they don't change a thing. So my hope is if I'm able to get an office and start this independent movement in Illinois, we can bring people more to that reasonable level of, ‘Yeah, I understand that we need funds to be able to help people.’”
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Juliana Stratton tries to make history, Don Tracy gives voice to state's GOP in race for Durbin Senate seat
entries.summary:
Self-described “fighter” Juliana Stratton is hoping to bring a new progressive voice to the U.S. Senate as she tries to take the reins from U.S Sen. Dick Durbin in a battle against former Illinois Republican Party Chair Don Tracy.

There is plenty of daylight between the two candidates — which was on full display during a lone debate last month on WTTW. Stratton’s platform includes a $25 minimum wage, abolishing ICE and she doesn’t support Chuck Schumer as the party’s leader. Her anti-President Trump messaging — including a “F*** Trump, vote Juliana” slogan — has been at the forefront of a campaign that began a day after Durbin announced his plans to retire.

Stratton is hoping she can carry over voter energy from a fiery primary campaign into the general election — which amounted to a lukewarm campaign battle. A Public Policy Polling poll in late September projected Stratton up by 13 points.

Stratton, a former mediator, was first elected to the Illinois House of Representatives in 2016 and has served as Gov. JB Pritzker’s lieutenant governor since 2018. She is credited for leading the Birth Equity Initiative, which helped address the racial disparity in Illinois' maternal mortality rates for Black women. She also helped to spearhead the Justice, Equity and Opportunity Initiative, with the goal of shifting the state’s criminal legal system towards more restorative programs.

Her campaign also touted her work in the Ag Connects Us All Initiative, which helped to highlight the ways in which the agriculture industry could address inequities and food security. It also served as a way to stay connected to the more rural areas of the state.

Illinois will see its fourth Black senator in the Senate if Stratton wins the reliably blue seat in November. She would also become the sixth Black woman to serve in the current Senate and the second Black woman to represent Illinois in the U.S. Senate.

Stratton defeated fundraising leader U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, Rep. Robin Kelly and eight other candidates in a contentious primary that included a late campaign surge and millions in support from Pritzker. She was also the first Democrat to announce a bid for Durbin’s seat, and announced Pritzker’s endorsement just two days later. The governor spent $10 million to help Stratton's primary campaign through a pro-Stratton PAC.

Although Pritzker has downplayed his support of Stratton, he'll be able to tout that he helped to elect a member of the Senate should she win.

In announcing her bid, Stratton touted her accomplishments as lieutenant governor, including raising the minimum wage, the state’s infrastructure accomplishments, gun safety laws and enshrining abortion laws in Illinois.

Republicans haven’t won a statewide seat in Illinois in 12 years, when Pritzker unseated GOP former Gov. Bruce Rauner, a close ally of Tracy. But Tracy says he’s running to give a voice to the millions of Republicans in the state.

Tracy is a Springfield attorney and businessman. He served as the chair of the Illinois Republican Party from 2021 until his resignation in July 2024. He is also the former chairman of the Illinois Gaming Board, appointed in 2015. Tracy pointed to Republican infighting for his exit from his chairmanship of the state GOP party in 2024 after three and a half years, a tenure that saw the party’s influence wane further in the state as its base moves further right. Tracy ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor in 2010 — and won a Democratic primary for a state Senate seat in 2002. He lost in the general election. Tracy was narrowly elected state GOP chair over pushback from hardline conservative leaders from rural areas downstate, where Trump remains immensely popular.

Tracy says he wants stricter border enforcement, upholding federal immigration laws and stronger support for law enforcement. He’s also supportive of Trump’s plan for a voter ID.

Tracy has tried to focus his Senate campaign on affordability and economic issues, but he has walked a fine line in discussing support for Trump. The president saw a bump in support in 2024, with his statewide vote growing to 45.3% in 2024, compared to 38.76%.

During the October debate, Tracy said “the jury’s still out on tariffs.”

“I like the fact that the president recognizes that we’ve been subsidizing the world, and we’ve been taken advantage of by the world with unfair trade practices out there, and so he’s trying to use, I think, tariffs as a tool, not an objective, but as a tool to reset world trade policy and make it a more level playing field," Tracy said.

He also called Operation Midway Blitz “ugly and chaotic,” but compared immigration enforcement in the Chicago area to that in Memphis, where he said things had “gone pretty well” because local authorities cooperated with federal immigration agents.

He blamed the violence on “massive resistance by the local authorities,” and he accused Americans of caring more about the deaths of four Americans at the hands of federal agents than to police shot in the line of duty.

“Certainly the immigration advocates don’t care about the thin blue line,” Tracy said.

entries.title: Patty García wants to move forward, as three other challengers vie for seat to replace Rep. 'Chuy' Garcia
entries.summary:
There has been no shortage of controversy in the 4th Congressional District, where U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” García’s last-minute decision to drop out of the primary race led him to helping his chief of staff quickly take his spot on the primary ballot.

Since then, Patty García — no relation to the congressman — fended off two independent candidates who railed on what they called a Democratic machine play, but ultimately failed to survive petition challenges with the Illinois State Board of Elections.

Lyons Mayor Christopher Getty is now running as the lone independent candidate. Lupe Castillo is the Republican candidate and Ed Hershey, a teacher, is running as the Working Class Party candidate.

Patty García has been ignoring the noise, building major Democratic support, both in Illinois and in Washington. And while she has repeatedly defended the ballot switch, which the congressman attributed to family and health reasons, she’s also asserted that voters on focused on other issues, including immigration and affordability. Many people in the district are still fearful of ICE and reluctant to apply for citizenship.

Patty García has been fully embraced by Illinois Democrats, and kicked off early voting in Little Village last week with Gov. JB Pritzker’s running mate Christian Mitchell and Latino elected officials and candidates. She’s also campaigning with Congressman García.

She has also racked up more than 175 endorsements from Democrats, including U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Lt. Gov Juliana Stratton and Rep. Delia Ramirez. She’s also backed by the Illinois AFL-CIO, Chicago Federation of Labor and SEIU Illinois State Council.

Getty has served as mayor of Lyons since 2009 and is also the supervisor of Lyons Township. He’s also a licensed insurance producer. Getty says his priorities include improving the cost of living, immigration and public safety and government accountability.

Getty in November wrote a scorching Chicago Tribune op-ed piece criticizing Congressman García for his last-minute decision not to run — and perhaps setting the stage for his own candidacy.

“It’s a move right out of the playbook of machine politics, anointing successors rather than letting the democratic process determine them,” Getty wrote in the piece.

Getty, who was elected mayor in 2009 at the age of 26, said he thinks being from the suburbs could be seen as a strength in the district that has traditionally been represented by Chicagoans.

Castillo says she’s running on a platform of “pro-family values and policies.” She says she’s the only candidate who “will protect women’s sports and girl’s bathrooms,” and who would support law enforcement over criminals. She’s also supportive of voter ID and school choice. She has lived in the district for 43 years.

Hershey has been teaching at Lindblom Math and Science Academy in West Englewood for 16 years and says his work in schools has shown him how a lack of resources can affect students. He’s also served as a union representative and ran for alderman of the 25th Ward in 2015.
