entries.title: Gabby Shanahan, Jessica Dixon Heitman square off in suburban statehouse race spurred by scandal
entries.summary:
A far southwest suburban legislative race could provide an indicator of just how much Springfield’s latest sexual harassment scandal is impacting Democrats who hold supermajorities in the Illinois General Assembly — and whether Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch has become a political liability for the party.

The race for the 97th District House seat would’ve been hotly contested even if disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, hadn’t been forced out amid allegations of misconduct over the summer.

But the battle in a rare purple district on Illinois’ grossly gerrymandered political map was tossed higher into the air over the summer with Benton’s resignation, which raised the broader question of why Welch backed his 2024 reelection despite being aware of a preceding complaint against Benton at the time.

Republican nominee Gabby Shanahan is making a second run for the office she lost to Benton by just four percentage points two years ago, sunk in no small part by the $1.4 million Welch directed to Benton’s campaign.

This time, Shanahan is aiming to unseat appointed state Rep. Jessica Dixon Heitman, the Plainfield Democrat whose campaign has received support from the Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House political committee to the tune of more than $1.6 million.

Dixon Heitman herself saw “red flags” in Benton’s office during a brief stint as a contract employee, she has said, but didn’t make a formal complaint.

Dixon Heitman told the Farmers Weekly Review of Will County that she respected the wishes of the young complainant who “was very opposed to filing any sort of report.”

Welch’s office was aware of allegations surfacing from Benton’s office, but he has claimed no choice but to continue backing Benton without a formal complaint to spur an investigation.

The speaker booted Benton from the caucus this February when another woman filed a complaint. A third woman’s complaint was detailed in a legislative watchdog’s report that prompted Benton to step down. He has denied wrongdoing.

Shanahan has said Dixon Heitman should’ve done more to flag Benton’s alleged misbehavior, while Illinois Republicans across the board have lambasted Welch’s handling of the case in addition to his own social media interactions. He has apologized for messages sent to a Benton complainant after the fact that left her uncomfortable.

Shanahan has also called on Dixon Heitman to pledge not to vote for Welch as speaker when the new General Assembly is sworn in next year. Dixon Heitman hasn’t said whether she’ll support him.

While state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, has slammed Welch over the case, no Democratic representatives have publicly called for him to give up the gavel, which is no lock for Welch to retain in January. Several representatives declined to join a sexual harassment working group assembled to address the issue by Welch, who is running unopposed for an eighth term in his west suburban district.

Welch himself took the speaker’s office in the wake of ex-House Speaker Michael Madigan’s downfall, which was precipitated by his own mishandling of sexual harassment allegations in his 13th Ward political organization almost a decade ago.

Still, the two working moms running for the 97th seat agree Springfield’s troubling culture of sexual harassment isn’t the top issue for voters in a district spanning most of Plainfield, part of Joliet and smaller portions of Aurora, Naperville, Bolingbrook, Oswego and Shorewood.

As is the case in most races this season, the most pressing concern is the rapidly rising cost of living, Dixon Heitman and Shanahan say.

“Families are working hard, but too many people feel like they're falling behind as the price of just about everything continues to rise,” Dixon Heitman, a former media relations consultant, said in a statement. “Voters want leaders who understand those challenges firsthand and are focused on helping people get ahead, not scoring political points.”

“You have a broad range of people that really want to be able to afford to live in the 97th District,” said Shanahan, a court-appointed special advocate for children in the Kendall County court system. “They need their property tax crisis address. They need the cost of living address, and they want somebody that is going to represent them with integrity and honesty.”
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Syed vs. Hills suburban state legislative race is one of the most expensive ever
entries.summary:
Republicans are not expected to make a dent in Democrats' supermajority in the Illinois General Assembly, but a multi-million-dollar suburban legislative race has turned into a fiery, closely watched contest in the lead-up to Election Day Tuesday.

In that race, state Rep. Nabeela Syed, a Democrat from Inverness, is challenging incumbent Republican Darby Hills of Barrington Hills for the Illinois Senate 26th District seat.

The $6.5 million raised makes it one of the most expensive contests in the history of the General Assembly, said Alisa Kaplan, executive director of Reform for Illinois.

Syed received at least $4.7 million in contributions, much of it from her party, while Hills has raised $1.8 million, said Kaplan, whose organization runs the Illinois Sunshine Database.

"The Democratic leadership wants to flip this seat, and it shows," Kaplan said.

Syed raised more than $3 million from the Democratic Party of Illinois and the Illinois Senate Democratic Fund, which is controlled by Illinois Senate President Don Harmon. She’s also raised substantial amounts of money from unions.

Darby’s last big contribution from her party was in August when the Illinois Senate Republican Campaign gave her $300,000.

Separate from Hills' own fundraising, a political action committee called the Strong Independent Leadership Committee formed last month to oppose Syed. It’s stated purpose is “ensuring only strong, independent leaders are elected by opposing extreme candidates,” according to a state filing.

Vince Foglia of North Barrington formed the political committee and contributed $500,000 to it.

Separately, Foglia and his family have also contributed $500,000 to Hills’ campaign.

Hills was appointed to fill out the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization.

Syed, 27, is completing her second term in the Illinois House after graduating from the University of California Berkeley in 2021, while Hills is completing the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization. Syed was the youngest woman and one of the only Muslims ever to be elected to the Illinois General Assembly.

Hills, 50, has raised Syed’s youth and experience as a campaign issue. In the final days, she’s called Syed “too extreme” to represent her district.

"I've represented the community for four years," Syed said in an interview. "I'm proud of my record. It's disingenuous to call that extreme."

A former prosecutor and 2021 Mrs. Illinois America, Hills was a village trustee before being appointed to McConchie’s seat. She has campaigned for public safety, especially related to children, lower taxes and government spending controls.

Syed, a Palatine native, said affordability and access to health care are among her top priorities.

Both candidates call for more oversight of data center development, a contentious issue across the state.

While Democrats see a potential to pick up suburban seats it only pads the big advantages they already have in the legislature.

Before Tuesday’s election, Democrats hold super-majorities in both the Illinois House (78-40) and Illinois Senate (40-19). Every Illinois House seat was up for election Nov. 3, while voters were slated to decide 39 state senate races, two thirds of the total members.

Elsewhere, Democrats were looking to unseat 52nd House District Republican Martin McLaughlin who faced Maria Peterson again.

In 2024, McLaughlin eked out a victory against Peterson, beating her by fewer than 50 votes.

Peterson cited affordability, environmental protection and safety atop of the issues she was focusing on, and pointed to her records as a lawyer doing advocacy work.

McLaughlin has said he’s focused on government spending and accountability.

More than a quarter of the members of the Illinois General Assembly represent Chicago or portions of the city, and the vast majority are Democrats.

Only one incumbent Democrat lost in March. State Rep. Jaime Andrade Jr. was beat in his primary for House District 40 by challenger and community activist Miguel Alvelo Rivera for the North Side seat. Alvelo Rivera is unopposed in Tuesday’s election.

Republicans saw an opportunity in another rematch where Republican Liz Bishop was challenging incumbent Democrat Amy “Murri” Briel in the 76th Illinois House District race in north central Illinois. The campaign includes some eyebrow-raising allegations.

Bishop, who lost to Briel in 2024 by less than 600 votes, released a recorded interview with a former staffer who alleged that Briel sexually harassed her, fed her prescription stimulant drugs and smoked pot while working as a lawmaker.

Briel denied the allegations and said a state legislative watchdog investigation concluded the claims were unfounded.

entries.title: Republicans face uphill battle in races for Illinois attorney general, comptroller, secretary of state
entries.summary:
Illinois’ statewide offices could end up Tuesday where they have been for decades — with a full slate of Democrats taking the reins.

The state hasn’t seen a Republican as secretary of state in nearly 30 years, as attorney general in more than 20 years or as comptroller for at least a decade.

A win by Alexi Giannoulias, however, would come with the complication that he’s also considered a front-runner for the fifth floor of City Hall. If he wins both races, it would allow fellow Tuesday night candidate Gov. JB Pritzker to appoint a secretary of state for the better part of a full term.

Secretary of State, Giannoulias vs. Harris

Giannoulias has focused on maintaining “momentum on modernization” on the campaign trail, while touting the introduction of online appointments for secretary of state office visits and the installation of DMV kiosks.

He faces Diane M. Harris, who unsuccessfully ran for State Senate as the Republican nominee in 2022 but landed the Republican nod for secretary of state by six points. Giannoulias and Harris split on age-based testing for drivers, as he rolled back testing requirements for elder drivers while she’s in favor of tests for all age groups.

On license plate readers, Harris said she would ensure the office followed state laws, while Giannoulias seeks to make his office’s audits of the technology more proactive. He also said he wants to establish pathways for accountability following searches of state data by federal immigration authorities searched state data and alleged abused by police.

His campaign has been propped up by millions of dollars in funds, being left with $21.85 million in cash on hand in the second quarter, with more pouring in as he announced his mayoral run. Harris raised more than $6,000 in the same span, nearly the same amount Giannoulias spent to hold a single fundraiser in April.

But no amount of money, nor his track record, allowed him to outrun the lingering question of his simultaneous run for mayor.

“The people deserve someone who’s committed to serving this state’s office,” Harris jabbed in a Sun-Times candidate questionnaire response.

Attorney General, Raoul vs. Fioretti

Former two-term 2nd Ward Ald. Robert Fioretti has an uphill battle against incumbent Attorney General Kwame Raoul, who won both his elections to the seat by a more than 11-point margin.

Raoul has served an elevated role in his second term. He, along with other states’ attorneys general, has successfully won the release of millions of dollars in federal dollars the Trump administration has tried to retract over sanctuary city policies, including funding for disaster relief funding and transportation.

Other lawsuits from his office have restored medical research funding cut by the Trump administration and reversed a Trump administration attempt to cut federal funding from medical institutions providing gender affirming care to patients under 19.

Fioretti meanwhile hasn’t held office since his second term in City Council ended in 2015, and has since unsuccessfully ran twice for mayor and Cook County state’s attorney, as well as a failed run at Cook County board president.

Fioretti cites his courtroom experience with the City of Chicago corporation counsel office, as well as his time as an assistant Illinois attorney general and alderman, as his qualifications for the state’s highest legal office.

Comptroller, Croke vs. Drew

Incumbent Susana Mendoza decided to put her efforts solely behind the Chicago mayor’s race, leaving an uncontested Republican Bryan Drew up against Democratic State Rep. Margaret Croke for the state’s chief financial office.

Croke, who was backed by a contingent of Springfield Democrats, including Gov. JB Pritzker, landed nearly 35% of the vote in a four-way split, beating out more progressive candidates. She pointed to her statehouse ties as a positive for the office, and cited her time on the House Revenue and Finance Committee and as chair of the Financial Institutions Committee as strengths heading into the state’s head financial office.

She raised $1.8 million in the primary, but has taken criticism from Drew for accepting money from Pritzker and billionaire business executive Michael Sacks. Drew, a private attorney and cafe owner, ended the first quarter of fundraising with just more than $54,000.

Both candidates called for increased transparency in the office with suggestions for new data sharing systems that allow people to track where their tax dollars are spent.

In response to the recent investigation of a South Side funeral home for mishandling of human remains, Croke backed moving the regulation of funeral home licensing solely under the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation.

entries.title: Bears RB D'Andre Swift gets 'hard yards' — and 3 TDs — vs. Seahawks
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Halfway across the country Monday night, Ayo Dosunmu was telling Timberwolves reporters that he liked to drive to the basket the way a running back would carry the ball. The Chicago-born Dosunmu, a former Bulls guard and a lifelong Bears fan, was asked if he tried to mimic the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ D’Andre Swift.</p><p>No, he joked — he’s more like former Vikings running back Adrian Peterson.</p><p>While Dosunmu was trying to score points with his new city, Swift was scoring three touchdowns in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/chargers-coach-jim-harbaugh-says-he-doesnt-want-to-trade-ex-bears-de-khalil-mack" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ 34-17 win Monday night against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks at Lumen Stadium.</p><p>The Bears’ running back wasn’t flashy — he averaged just 2.6 yards per carry and never had a run longer than seven yards — but he remained the metronome on which the Bears’ offense is calibrated.</p><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams’ Year 3 leap doesn’t happen without the steadiness of Swift. The defense doesn’t stay fresh without the Bears running clock with their running game, which has contributed to their league-best time of possession. And coach Ben Johnson’s creativity doesn’t get unleashed unless he can trust his running back.</p><p>“I know he didn't have a ton of yards, but 27 attempts and three touchdowns, every single yard was earned by him,” Johnson said. “Those are hard yards to come by.”</p><p>The Seahawks entered the game allowing the fewest total yards and the sixth-fewest rushing yards per game in the NFL. The game was a grind.</p><p>Swift ran for three touchdowns for just the second time in his career, giving him a whopping 10 on the season. The last Bears running back that could say that through eight games was Rick Casares in 1956.</p><p>He’s had a rushing touchdown in his fourth-straight game for the second time in his Bears career. The last Bear who could say that was Neal Anderson, most recently in 1990.</p><p>And while invoking this name might be sacrilege, it’s true nonetheless: Swift has more rushing touchdowns this season than Walter Payton did in eight of his 13 seasons with the Bears.</p><p>“We just came into the game with a mindset of, we'll just take our four [yards] as far as the run game goes,” right tackle Darnell Wright said. “And then when the defense opens up the pass game, we look to Caleb and the receivers and how they play.”:</p><p>Johnson insisted the Bears keep pounding even after Swift went into the locker room at halftime with just 11 carries for 26 yards and no touchdowns. He had 16 carries for 43 yards and three rushing scores in the second half.</p><p>“Shoutout to Ben for sticking with the run against a great opponent,” Swift said. “[The Seahawks] made it tough tonight. When we got down to the red zone, O-line, receivers did their job.”</p><p>In doing so, the Bears shined in an area that earlier in the season was a weakness. Monday night, they scored touchdowns all four times they went inside the Seahawks’ 20.The Bears went 3-for-4 the week before and 2-for-3 in Williams’ return in Atlanta.</p><p>Swift’s workload might shrink whenever the Bears get Kyle Monangai back. He seemed to be their preferred short-yardage back before suffering a turf toe injury in Week 4 against the Jets.</p><p>Swift proved adept in his absence. In the four games Monangai has missed, Swift has run for a staggering seven touchdowns. Only six NFL running backs have more than seven touchdowns all year.</p><p>Even more importantly, Swift hasn’t fumbled since he was benched toward the end of Week 4 for losing his second fumble of the year. Swift leads the league in touchdown runs and ranks 12<sup>th</sup> with 68.1 yards per game.</p><p>Monday night, he had as many touchdowns in one half as any Bears running back or wide receiver has all year, combined.</p><p>“We had our work cut out for us,” Swift said. “I’m just proud of the way we fought in all three phases.”</p>

Irving Park Rd., about 12:10 a.m., according to police and sources. </p><p>The unidentified man, who suffered burns to his body and head injuries, was dead on the scene, police said. </p><p>No one was arrested. </p><p>Area 5 detectives are conducting a homicide investigation. </p>

entries.title: Brittany Bailey Preston, wife of local state senator, runs unopposed in South Side’s District 9a in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 9a neighborhoods: Auburn Gresham, West Englewood, Englewood, New City, Ashburn, Washington Heights 

Voters in this South Side district will have a new representative — with a familiar last name — on Chicago’s school board because the current member, who was appointed by the mayor, was removed from the ballot in July.

Brittany Bailey Preston, the wife of state Sen. Willie Preston, whose district covers part of the same South Side territory, is effectively guaranteed the seat because she is the sole candidate in the race.

Angel Velez, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s appointee to District 9a, filed to run for election but was removed from the ballot after a large percentage of his signatures were challenged and invalidated.

The majority-Black district includes a mix of 47 neighborhood, charter and magnet schools serving mostly Black and Hispanic students. The area also has one of the lowest percentages of schools that earned either “exemplary” or “commendable” designations last year from the state — the top two ratings — across the city. A number of schools here have struggled with declining enrollment over the past 15 years.

The district also has one of the lowest percentages citywide of CPS students choosing neighborhood schools. Some 32% of students in 9a chose their neighborhood elementary and high schools compared to 46% systemwide, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat.

This seat was previously held by Frank Thomas, who resigned in June 2025, and was later replaced by Velez. But after being removed from the ballot, Velez said he would not pursue a write-in candidacy.

Preston’s biggest campaign donation came from the SEIU Illinois Council political action committee, which endorsed her. Her campaign was also supported by groups who oppose the Chicago Teachers Union and are proponents of school choice and charter schools, including The Urban Center, the Common Ground Collective and the Illinois Network of Charter Schools.

entries.title: Every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s immigration blitz
entries.summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago have accused 33 known defendants of nonimmigration crimes tied to Operation Midway Blitz. Many were accused of assaulting or resisting federal agents or officers.</p><p>Two defendants have pleaded guilty. Twenty-seven have been cleared. Grand jurors refused to indict at least three of the 27, and another member of that group was found not guilty at trial.</p><p>Three of the 27 saw their charges dropped through a deferred-prosecution agreement. Under the terms of such a deal, prosecutors agree to drop charges if a defendant abides by certain terms over a set period of time. Six Midway Blitz defendants struck such a deal, and three are still pending.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times is tracking all of the known criminal cases tied to Operation Midway Blitz:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-table" data-src="visualisation/27349648"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27349648/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="table visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><div class="PageListO" data-module data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-bb0000" name="list-bb0000"></a> <div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> Latest from Jon Seidel </div> </div> </div> <div class="PageListO-items"> <div class="PageListO-items-row"> <div class="PageListO-items-column" data-with-borders> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" >'Broadview 6' case heats up again as ex-FBI boss sues, top federal prosecutor ordered to testify</a> </div> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/02/broadview-six-boutros-perry" >Chicago's top federal prosecutor ordered to testify under oath in 'Broadview 6' case</a> </div> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/02/broadview-six-depodesta-boutros-kat-abughazaleh" >Former FBI boss’ lawsuit undermines Boutros’ denial of Washington’s role in ‘Broadview 6’ case</a> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Millions of American women don't want kids — one stands up to explain why
entries.summary: <p>The American birthrate has fallen to historic lows, and Bailey Swilley isn't helping any. Which is ironic.</p><p>"I love babies," said the Brooklyn-based comedian/storyteller. "That's the thing. I love babies. I like kids."</p><p>Fair enough. I love bread, yet don't want to be a baker.</p><p>"I don't see myself as a parent," she said. "I don't see myself in that role."</p><p>She was a lot of company. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recently announced a fertility rate of 1.6 children per American woman — well below the replacement level of 2.1. I'd been brooding on this for a while when the email from a publicist hit my in-box, slugged, "NOV 21: Hit NYC Fringe Show in Chicago — Bailey Swilley's "A Baby For Me? No Thank You, Please!"</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5b0000" name="module-5b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Approaching random women and asking why they don't want to have children seems a recipe for a quick trip to human resources. But here was an opportunity. About a third of young women don't want kids. What soured Swilley on the prospect?</p><p>"I am an older sister, my brother is five years younger," said Swilley, who grew up in Memphis. "Older enough to remember watching my parents parent him and me, and thinking, 'Yuck. I don't think that's for me. I just don't see myself in this. Not what I aspire to.'"</p><p>Inherent revulsion with parenthood doesn't usually make the traditional list of reasons people don't want children — jittery economy, lack of suitable partners, the generally fraught future. Swilley mentioned the term "body horror" — she has a routine about a doctor hunting for part of a broken IUD — as well as the "ring of fire," which I thought had to do with volcanic activity in the Pacific, but is also a phrase associated with the pain of childbirth.</p><p>Swilley is married — I assumed her husband is on board with her determined childlessness.</p><p>"We're on the same page," she said. "I bring it up a lot. I ask him. All of his friends have kids, more his friends than mine. We spend at lot of time with his friends' kids. Afterwards, I'll check in, 'Did you feel anything? Feel that should be something we do?' We have those check-ins a lot, and always land at, No."</p><p>Other folks' kids will do that. I distinctly remember the shock of being childless and visiting friends who had just had children, to find them sitting sunken-eyed in the middle of their shattered apartments, their padded coffee tables and plastic safety gates and gadgets, spattered with spit up and splotches of green and orange baby food, smiling these serene, exhausted, souls-among-the-damned-in-hell grins and urging us to follow them over the cliff into their zombie cult.</p><p>I asked Swilley if she worries, having planted her flag so publicly against ever having children, that she may someday change her mind.</p><p>"A lot of women talk about the concept of being John Mulvaney," she said. "The comedian John Mulvaney was all about 'We never want kids. Me and my wife love our lives, child-free.' Then all of a sudden he left his wife and got this really hot woman pregnant."</p><p>Here she lets out a laugh.</p><p>"Oh my God, you can think you're on the same page and the rug gets swept out from under you. That's something lurking in a lot of child-free women's minds."</p><p>Well, yes, life will yank that old rug out from under you. I don't think either my wife or I planned on grinding away as mid-60-ish custodians maintaining a decaying 125-year-old, five-bedroom farmhouse with a formal dining room, so it'll be available for the pleasure of children and grandchildren for a few days out of every month. Yet here we are.</p><p>Being a parent is hard work, and not for everybody. Space here is limited, and I can only touch on my conversation with Swilley. If you want to hear more, she's at the <a class="Link" href="https://thedentheatre.com/performances/2026/11/21/a-baby-for-me-no-thank-you-please-the-den-theatre-comedy-club-chicago" target="_blank" >Den Theatre</a>, 1331 N. Milwaukee Avenue on Nov. 21, for two shows, 7 and 9 p.m. </p><p>I asked Swilley if she worried she'd be inspiring audience members not to have children — basically responsible for children not being born into the world.</p><p>"No, I don't thinks so," she said. "It's not me trying to convince anyone. This is my true belief. I believe it's something that's inherently in you, or not. I was just born with the feeling that it just wasn't for me. A lot of people know deep down whether it's for them or not."</p><p>"Ultimately, you're bringing a stranger into the world." she continued, and I thought, <i>Yeah, but they don't stay a stranger for long...</i> Which is the joy, and the burden.</p>

entries.title: Burglary crew carried out nearly 30 thefts in Beverly, Lincoln Park in October
entries.summary: <p>A group of at least four burglars carried out nearly 30 thefts throughout October, according to Chicago police. </p><p>In each of the 29 thefts, the burglars used rocks and sledgehammers to shatter storefront windows and took cash registers from inside before fleeing in stolen vehicles, police said. </p><p>Businesses in Beverly and Lincoln Park were the hardest hit, with West Englewood, Gresham, Brainard and North Center among other areas impacted by the burglaries, officials said.</p><p>Thirteen of the thefts happened around 4 a.m. Oct. 27 in the 2400 and 2500 blocks of North Clark Street and an additional six occurred around 3:45 a.m. Oct. 15 in the 2100 block of West 95th Street, police said. </p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to call Area 1 detectives at 312-747-8384, Area 2 detectives at 312-747-8273 or Area 3 detectives at 312-744-8263. </p>

entries.title: Man charged after confrontation, fight with firefighter, police in Greater Grand Crossing over weekend
entries.summary: <p>A West Side man was charged with battering a firefighter who moments later bashed him with a blunt object Sunday morning during a confrontation in Greater Grand Crossing on the South Side. </p><p>Lamar Brown, 32, was charged with aggravated battery and aggravated assault of a firefighter, Chicago police said. He was also wanted on eight warrants. </p><p>Brown allegedly assaulted an on-duty firefighter around 11:45 a.m. Sunday in the 7300 block of South Maryland Avenue, police said. </p><p>Police used a taser after Brown ignored verbal commands, but efforts were "ineffective," police said in a statement. </p><p>As Brown continued toward the firefighter, he used a blunt object to strike Brown, who was then arrested, police said. </p><p>Brown, of Austin, was scheduled to appear in court Tuesday for a detention hearing. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Bulls forward Matas Buzelis trying to find his way one fight at a time
entries.summary: <p>PHILADELPHIA – Matas Buzelis was doing a lot of fighting late Monday night.</p><p>Fighting to keep his confidence up, fighting to figure out his place in the Bulls offense, fighting to make sure he chose his words wisely in describing his early-season inconsistencies.</p><p>A fight that remains ongoing.</p><p>Buzelis came into the 2026-27 campaign on an upward trajectory. In Year 2 alone, he emerged as one of the team’s best scorers with an elite combination of shot-blocking and three-point shooting that few in the league have been capable of.</p><p>Through seven games on a one-win team, Buzelis is averaging 13 points per game, trying to play in a new system with new teammates – including the new shiny toy that is standout rookie Caleb Wilson – and on far too many half-court offensive sets finds himself stuck in the corner.</p><p>No one puts Buzelis in a corner.</p><p>“If you can recall, every one of my seasons, like first and second (years), they were tough (at the start),” Buzelis said. “It was difficult. You know, new guys coming in … it makes it harder. That’s just God putting me in positions where there’s challenges all the time, and I can achieve anything I want. I worked extremely hard this summer. Sometimes you work hard and you think you’ll get the results. Right now, you got to really focus in on what you can control and what you can do out there.”</p><p>He’s not wrong about finding his way throughout a season. As a rookie, he wasn’t even playing consistently pre-All-Star break and went on to finish the final 27 games of that year averaging 13 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.1 blocks per game.</p><p>Last year, he jumped up almost four points per game from first half to second half, improving his rebounding and shot blocking along the way.</p><p>But Year 3 wasn’t supposed to have a slow start for the 6-foot-8 forward. He was supposed to be Robin to Wilson’s Batman on a bad day. No one asked for Flash.</p><p>But yet that’s what Buzelis is right now. He flashed in the loss to the Wizards and then in a six-point loss to New York, while hitting a season downer Monday night in Philadelphia, scoring four points and adding five turnovers.</p><p>His message to the doubters – and that group has been growing – is a simple one: “It’s all a process. Figuring out when to attack, when to shoot, it’s all different for me, but I’ll get it. It’s a matter of time.”</p><p>And while some Bulls fans and social media want to cast stones, the Bulls locker room isn’t even close to selling their Buzelis stock. Maybe because he’s not the only one trying to find his way.</p><p>“In the halfcourt, and I’ve spoken to it before, we have multiple guys that can be offensive weapons for us, so trying to balance that attack,” point guard Josh Giddey said. “Last year we didn’t have guys like Norm (Powell) and Caleb that can get you 20 at will. We’re all learning how to play with each other. Whether you’re saying his role is different or not, (Buzelis is) still that same super-talented player that you guys saw last year. It’s my responsibility to help get him back on track.”</p><p>And his coach’s. Not an easy thing to do just seven games in for Tiago Splitter. He has a shooting star in Wilson that he doesn’t want to lasso in any way but also make sure that the supporting actors are getting their moments in the spotlight too.</p><p>If that’s not handled right a locker room can splinter.</p><p>Luckily, Buzelis is not a me-first guy, understanding the team works better when he’s playing well, but it’s a group that all needs each other.</p><p>Could that be found playing with the second unit and getting put in more familiar actions? Maybe, but a fight for another day.</p><p>“I just got to get into a flow, man,” Buzelis said. “That’s all I need to get it going.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>A 21-year-old woman from Chicago was killed during a shooting attack Monday at a Hammond, Ind. Walmart, officials announced Tuesday. </p><p>An autopsy determined Dakota Norwood died of multiple gunshot wounds and her death was ruled a homicide, according to a statement from the Lake County coroner's office. </p><p>Norwood was shot about 9:35 a.m. Monday at Walmart, 1100 S. 5th Ave. in Hammond, and she was pronounced dead at 10:27 a.m., according to the statement. <br></p>

entries.title: New IHSA bylaw proposals would put public and private schools in separate state tournaments
entries.summary: <p>Until now, the dispute between public and private schools over competitive balance played out in press conferences and postgame interviews. Mount Carmel football coach Jordan Lynch and Batavia football coach Dennis Piron both regularly offered juicy quotes that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/19/ihsa-high-school-football-mount-carmel-batavia-private-school" >presented their sides of the issue</a>.</p><p>The time for empty talk has passed. Over the next six weeks, schools across the state will discuss several possible rule changes and state tournament format tweaks that could change the landscape of high school sports in Illinois.</p><p>The ongoing battle between public and private schools over an alleged “private school competitive advantage” is at the center of the two most significant bylaw proposals the Illinois High School Association released on Tuesday. The West Suburban Conference submitted both, and it includes Downers Grove North and South, Proviso East and West, Hinsdale Central and South, Leyden, Morton, Addison Trail, Willowbrook, York, Lyons, Glenbard West and Oak Park.</p><p>Proposal 8, submitted by the West Suburban, creates separate classes for boundary (public) and non-boundary (private and magnet) schools in the state tournaments. Under this format, public and private schools would no longer compete for the same state championships.</p><p>In four-class sports, there would be three classes for boundary schools and one class for non-boundary schools. In football, there would be six boundary classes and two non-boundary classes.</p><p>Under this proposed system, a basketball state championship game between Young and Glenbard West could not happen. A football state championship game between Maine South and Loyola would be impossible. Each of the schools mentioned would face similar schools and win separate state championships.</p><p>Proposal 15, also submitted by the West Suburban, creates separate paths to the state finals for boundary and non-boundary schools. Boundary and non-boundary schools would have separate sectionals and supersectionals, and one non-boundary team would advance to the state semifinals.</p><p>So basically, only one private/non-boundary public school would be allowed in the state semifinals in each class every year.</p><p>Under this proposed system, schools like Brother Rice, Mount Carmel and Lane would be placed in a separate supersectional, and the winning team would advance directly to the state semifinals in football and basketball. State championships between traditional public schools and non-boundary schools would be possible. Still, only one non-boundary school would be in the state finals in every class and sport.</p><p>Downers Grove North AD Dave Rose, who wrote Proposal 8 and 15, declined to comment specifically on the bylaws, telling the Sun-Times that, “the proposal is still very early in the process, and I'd like to give a chance to be discussed at the town hall meetings in November before talking through it.”</p><p>Athletic directors at Lyons, Hinsdale Central, Downers Grove South and York did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>According to a source, the West Suburban is expected to listen to feedback at IHSA town hall meetings across the state and then pull back the less popular proposal.</p><p>“St. Laurence and most private schools are in favor of keeping it the way it is,” St. Laurence AD and Catholic League vice president Tim Chandler said. “There are sports where private schools do pretty well and sports where we don’t do well. The focus always seems to be on the sports that the private schools have a good season in.”</p><p>Chandler said that Proposal 8, which separates the private and public schools into different state tournaments, is a non-starter.</p><p>“Private schools would have a decision to make in that situation,” Chandler said. “If we are going to be on our own anyway, would we do it under the IHSA or under our own terms with our own transfer bylaws?”</p><p>“I believe the four best schools should be at state, whether that is private schools or public schools. Restricting access for private schools and guaranteeing one spot doesn’t make sense. There might be sports where four public schools should be at state, and you are taking an opportunity away from a public school by guaranteeing a private school spot.</p><p>“There are a ton of small, non-boundary schools that have no business competing with Mount Carmel and Loyola in sports. That’s not right.”</p><p>Several sources have confirmed to the Sun-Times that the IHSA could push through Proposal 15 without a vote from the schools. Chandler has heard the same, and says the Catholic League would prefer that scenario. The IHSA is believed to prefer keeping private and public schools competing for the same state titles.</p><p>“There has been some talk about the [IHSA board] doing this under board policy instead of it being a bylaw,” Chandler said. “So then the board would have the ability to tweak it a little bit easier. Like what they have done with the current classification stuff. It would be better to see something come through that way.”</p><p><b>Other notable bylaw proposals:</b></p><p><b>Proposal 0 (already on the ballot):</b> Modifies the multiplier from 1.65 to 2.5. Non-boundary school enrollment will be multiplied by 2.5; this would send private schools and magnet schools into larger classes.</p><p><b>Proposal 2:</b> Increases the percentage of votes needed to pass a bylaw amendment from a simple majority to a 2/3 supermajority. This would make it more difficult to pass new bylaws.</p><p><b>Proposal 12:</b> Modifies transfer eligibility to allow students full eligibility for their first transfer before the start of their sophomore school year. This would basically allow one free transfer with no sitting out during a student’s first year of high school.</p><p><b>Proposal 16:</b> Restores the football setup the state used in 2025-26, rolling back the playoff expansion.</p>

entries.title: Parking attendants strike at O'Hare, McCormick Place, Hyatt Regency
entries.summary: <p>Parking attendants formed picket lines Tuesday at O'Hare Airport, McCormick Place and the Hyatt Regency as their union accused parking operators of bargaining in bad faith.</p><p>Members of Teamsters Local 727 began striking at 5:30 a.m. at the three locations, a union spokesperson said. The union represents nearly 1,200 members who staff parking garages across the city. They've been bargaining with the Chicago Parking Association over a contract that expired last week, when 98% of voting members authorized a strike.</p><p>The picket could potentially expand to other parking garages, such as at Navy Pier, according to the Teamsters.</p><p>Parking operations continued normally at O'Hare despite the picket, according to the Chicago Department of Aviation, which operates O'Hare.</p><p>McCormick Place's parking garages were also operating as usual, according to a spokesperson. Events and conventions will continue as planned, the spokesperson said. Representatives for Hyatt Regency did not immediately comment.</p><p>The Teamster's parking attendants recently voted down the operator's last contract proposal. The Teamsters, in a statement, said the proposal was presented as a "disrespectful 'last, best, and final' offer." The union accused the operators with refusing to bargain, failing to provide information, and making "unilateral changes to working conditions, retaliation, and unlawful surveillance."</p><p>A Chicago Parking Association spokesperson defended the contract proposal as "unprecedented" and "one of the most generous compensation packages in the parking industry nationwide." The association's five-year contract offer includes an overall 27% increase in wages and benefits, and a 7% wage increases in the first year, according to the spokesperson.</p><p>The proposal also includes a new retiree healthcare benefit and more paid time off. "We believe the offer on the table represents a substantial commitment to our employees and demonstrates just how far we are willing to go to reach a fair agreement," the spokesperson said.</p>
entries.author: David Struett

entries.title: Advocates say a loophole in an Illinois contract allows ICE to access data for immigration enforcement
entries.summary: <p>A multimillion-dollar contract with Appriss Insights LLC, which runs the state’s crime victim notification system, contains a provision that allows the company to share jail data with third parties, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, immigrant advocates say.</p><p>The state’s victim-notification system known as VINE alerts crime victims when someone is released from jail, transferred or experiences a change in custody status. Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul signed the current contract with Appriss in May 2021, initially committing approximately $6.07 million. The contract runs through June 2028.</p><p>A clause in that contract allows Appriss to share jail records with third parties. Privacy advocates warn this creates a pathway for information collected by Illinois jails to enter commercial databases used by ICE to identify and locate people for immigration enforcement.</p><p>Illinois’ sanctuary laws limit state and local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration authorities— including sharing information about anyone held at a local jail or prison — unless that person has a federal criminal warrant. But advocates say even though the state isn’t sharing this information directly, the loophole in the state’s contract offers a back door around the sanctuary laws.</p><p>“This is why we’ve been raising alarms for years,” Jacinta González, a former policy director at Mijente who is now head of programs at MediaJustice, told the Sun-Times in June. “When these loopholes are allowed to exist, they’re going to lead to concrete harm. They’re going to lead to people being detained and people being deported.</p><h3><b>How ICE uses jail records</b></h3><p>Federal procurement records show that in 2021, ICE sought access to Appriss records that contained information about bookings and incarcerations from more than 2,800 jails and correctional facilities nationwide. In 2022, The Guardian <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/apr/19/us-immigration-agency-data-loophole-information-deportation-targets" target="_blank" ><u>reported</u></a> that ICE paid about $4.8 million to access Appriss data.</p><p>As of November 2024, 88 county jails, 96 court systems and 31 Illinois Department of Corrections-affiliated facilities participate in the statewide victim-notification system, according to a report from the attorney general’s office.</p><p>Privacy advocates have argued for years that data provided to Appriss could move beyond state and county systems and into commercial databases like LexisNexis that are accessible to agencies like ICE. They allege ICE is able to access information that includes names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, custody status dates, release information, court hearing details and other sensitive personal data. Advocates say ICE’s contract with LexisNexis includes an add-on for a database called Justice Intelligence, a product offered by Appriss that collects release data from U.S. jails and prisons and makes it easily searchable.</p><p>“Basically, this is a loophole paragraph,” said Steven J. Kochevar, an attorney and law fellow at the University of Chicago, who has reviewed the state’s contract. Kochevar said the language in the contract leaves unclear exactly how Appriss may use the data it collects.</p><p>Without effective restrictions, companies can combine government records with information from other sources into commercial databases sold to customers, including government agencies, he explained.</p><p>“They package it and they sell it through these systems like LexisNexis,” he said.</p><p>Such databases can combine booking records with addresses and other personal information, creating profiles of people regardless of immigration status, including those arrested but never convicted.</p><p>“It’s not like one straight pipeline,” Kochevar said. “They [ICE] get a bunch of data in a lot of different ways.”</p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office said they were committed to protecting residents’ information from improper use, including for immigration enforcement.</p><p>“We are engaged in ongoing conversations with Appriss Insights LLC,” the spokesperson said.</p><p>The attorney general’s office did not say whether information from the statewide system had reached ICE and they did not identify any specific restrictions preventing access to the data. The office would not answer questions about whether the attorney general plans to change or retain the contract’s data-sharing provision.</p><p>Appriss also did not respond to questions about its contract with the state.</p><h3><b>Cook County as a model</b></h3><p>Last month, Cook County moved to strengthen protections against this type of data sharing with ICE. Commissioners approved an <a class="Link" href="https://cook-county.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?FullText=1&GUID=DF64E62B-EA79-4C99-8E2E-1F8D76C323AC&ID=8236765&Options&Search&u" target="_blank" ><u>ordinance</u></a> restricting how county employees and contractors share residents’ information with ICE and data brokers.</p><p>For Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, the county ordinance addresses a basic concern: information residents provide to government offices being used to target them.</p><p>“We wanted to make sure that that information that we are providing to the county — at the very least, to county offices — does not get weaponized against us for immigration enforcement purposes,” he said.</p><p>Tsao said Cook County’s ordinance could provide a model for restrictions elsewhere in Illinois.</p><p>Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law said the ordinance doesn’t solve the problem of data sharing elsewhere in Illinois.</p><p>“The fact remains that this company is still obtaining the personal information of people across other parts of Illinois, and that information is being shared with ICE through this contract,” Rivera said. “So there’s a lot of work to do.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div entries.title: Ex-Cubs managers Dusty Baker, Lou Piniella, Joe Maddon on ‘Contemporary Baseball Era’ Hall of Fame ballot
entries.summary: <p>Only one of them guided the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs </a>to a World Series championship, but a trio of recent North Side skippers could find themselves in the Hall of Fame next summer.</p><p>Three of the team’s last eight managers — Dusty Baker, Lou Piniella and Joe Maddon — are among the eight candidates on the Hall of Fame’s “Contemporary Baseball Era” non-player ballot, and a committee will vote on whether any will be part of next year’s Hall of Fame class, with voting results announced Dec. 6.</p><p>All three managers were splashy hires made with the intention of breaking the Cubs’ infamously lengthy championship drought dating back to 1908, and though Maddon was the one who got that job done, all three helmed teams that brought playoff baseball to Wrigley Field.</p><p>Baker came first, hired ahead of a 2003 campaign that saw the Cubs win a division title for the first time since the 1980s. That year’s run ended in the NLCS against the Marlins, the Cubs five outs away from a pennant only for disaster to strike in the now-legendary Steve Bartman Game.</p><p>Baker came to the Cubs after a decade managing the Giants, which culminated in him guiding that team to an NL pennant in 2002. After his four seasons on the North Side — which included just the single playoff appearance — he managed a dozen more major league seasons for the Reds, Nationals and Astros, finally capturing a World Series title with the Astros in 2022.</p><p>Piniella was the Cubs’ next attempt at bringing in a high-profile manager to end the drought, and he led the team to back-to-back division titles in his first two seasons, 2007 and 2008. The 97-win season under Piniella’s watch in 2008 was the franchise’s highest win total since their pennant-winning campaign in 1945.</p><p>But like Baker’s best days as a manager came elsewhere, the same is true for Piniella, whose fourth season with the Cubs in 2010 was the last of 23 as a big league skipper. He managed the Yankees and won the 1990 World Series as the Reds’ manager before a decade-long tenure helming the Mariners, during which he presided over a 116-win team in 2001 that still holds the major league record for the most wins in a season.</p><p>Maddon holds the distinction of the only manager to win a World Series with the Cubs in the last century, guiding the team to baseball’s promised land in 2016. He only managed the Cubs for five seasons — roughly half the time he spent at the helm of the Rays, taking that team to its first World Series appearance in 2008 — but made four trips to the postseason and three consecutive trips to the NLCS.</p><p>The trio joins one other former manager, Bruce Bochy, on the ballot, and of all the former skippers, Bochy has far and away the best case as a four-time World Series winner as manager of the Giants and Rangers.</p><p>Sandy Alderson, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner and Bill White are also on this year’s ballot.</p>

entries.title: Saint Knick: Former Stevenson star Jalen Brunson has year he couldn't have imagined
entries.summary: <p>Jalen Brunson could’ve been a Bull.</p><p>Not that he should’ve been a Bull. The Mavericks drafted Brunson with the third pick of the second round in 2018. But the Bulls had two first-round picks that year, and they chose Wendell Carter Jr. at No. 7 and Chandler Hutchinson at No. 22.</p><p>If they knew then what they know now — Brunson went 11 picks after Hutchinson, who played four nondescript NBA seasons — the Bulls might’ve wanted Brunson around.</p><p>And what fun that would’ve been. At Stevenson High School, Brunson was the Sun-Times’ Player of the Year in 2014 and ’15. His father, Rick, played two seasons for the Bulls (2002-04) and was an assistant on coach Tom Thibodeau’s staff in 2010-13.</p><p>But the Mavs took Brunson, and in 2022, he signed with the Knicks, who, for those of a certain age, make him a sworn enemy of the Bulls.</p><p>To dislike Brunson, though, is to dislike ice cream, puppies and rainbows. Even the Knicks as a team became likable last season on their way to the franchise’s first NBA title since 1973. For Brunson’s sake, it was best the Bulls didn’t draft him, because he wasn’t winning anything here.</p><p>And he wouldn’t have had the amazing six-month run he just had, either.</p><p>Brunson led the Knicks to the title and earned Finals MVP honors in June, becoming a legend in a city that had yearned for basketball glory. In September, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nba/2026/09/09/jalen-brunson-stevenson-host-saturday-night-live-season-premiere" >he hosted “Saturday Night Live,” </a>joining Michael Jordan among the handful of NBA greats to do so.</p><p>And on Thursday, he’ll appear on NBC’s “Law & Order: SVU” as Detective Madison — get it? — with show mainstay and Knicks superfan Mariska Hargitay.</p><p>“I thought I would be able to call myself a champion at some point in whatever role I was playing,” Brunson said last week after the Knicks beat the Bulls at the United Center. “But to say that I thought I’d have this type of year, I would be lying to you if I said I had a thought.”</p><p>Don’t expect Brunson to give up dribbling for acting anytime soon, even though he doesn’t quite fit the prototype for an NBA player — and that’s coming from his coach.</p><p>“You look at this guy, and he’s not 6-7, he’s not athletic, he’s not quick,” Mike Brown said. “You can go down the line in natural physical tools that a lot of guys have, but his determination, his competitive spirit, his will, his toughness, it makes him an unbelievable basketball player.”</p><div class="Enhancement" He has finished in the top five for Clutch Player of the Year — aka the Jerry West Trophy — in four consecutive years, winning in 2025.</p><p>He did, however, seem to need some home cooking last week when he entered the game against the Bulls in a shooting slump. In the stadium that Jordan built and Brunson visited often as a kid, he found his touch, shooting 52% from the field and 60% from three-point range for a season-high 38 points. He’ll face the Bulls again Wednesday at Madison Square Garden.</p><p>“I was just happy to be able to finally get over the hump,” Brunson said. “I felt like I was putting a lot of unnecessary commentary in my head. But seeing the ball going the way it did got me out of my mental state and put me back in a good state.”</p><p>Literally and figuratively. Brunson said he has many fond memories from the United Center. He watched the Bulls’ Derrick Rose and the Heat’s LeBron James battle in the 2011 Eastern Conference finals.</p><p>“I remember exactly where we used to sit,” he said.</p><p>He met countless players, including the late Kobe Bryant.</p><p>“It was in that hallway,” he said, nodding toward the area outside the visitors’ locker room.</p><p>He also met Rose, with whom Brunson reconnected after the game. After making a shot late in the game, Brunson appeared to point toward Rose. Later, he clarified that he was pointing at Rose’s oldest son, PJ, who’s 14.</p><p>“It’s crazy to see how old he is now,” Brunson said. “The relationship I have with [Rose] and his family, I feel like the feeling is mutual. I’m just happy to have that guy as a mentor and personally I can talk to, and I just really look up to, as well.”</p><p>Rose was on his fourth team, the Timberwolves, when Brunson entered the league. So a Bulls backcourt of Brunson and Rose was never in the cards. But after seeing what Brunson has become with the Knicks — the Knicks! — it’s hard not to be envious of what they have with one of our own.</p><p>“An MVP-caliber basketball player,” Brown said. “I hope he gets recognition for that this year because his will is off the charts.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs’ front office loses another key member as Mariners hire farm director Jason Kanzler as new manager
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs’</a> front office has lost another key member.</p><p>Not long after assistant general manager Jared Banner left to become the Orioles’ new GM, player-development director Jason Kanzler was hired away as the Mariners’ new manager Tuesday.</p><p>Kanzler was the Cubs’ farm chief for the last three seasons, a stint that followed a half decade with the Astros, during which he was a coach on the major league staff for two seasons.</p><p>The 36-year-old Kanzler becomes the second youngest manager in the major leagues, older than only Nationals skipper Blake Butera, who is 34.</p><p>Whether the Cubs — who started last season with three assistant GMs — fill Banner’s position remains to be seen. But they obviously need to find a replacement for Kanzler as the head of their player-development department.</p><p>The hires into prominent positions by other clubs show the Cubs had some desirable talent as part of their brain’s trust.</p><p>But now two key pieces are gone as Jed Hoyer & Co. begin an important offseason in which pitching will be the primary focus, a focus that extends beyond external acquisitions and includes evaluating how the Cubs work to develop pitching in the minor leagues, Kanzler’s now-former area of responsibility.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: This recipe for a kimchi seafood pot keeps chef Esther Choi’s mom coming back for more
entries.summary: <p>Like my recipes for Kimchi Bolognese and Kimchi Mac and Beef, this dish from my cookbook “Hand Taste: Cook Like a Korean Grandmother” is part of my Korean Italian American repertoire.</p><p>And out of them all, this Kimchi Seafood Pot is my mom's favorite. I made it for her once just for fun, and now she asks me to make it all the time. It's all about seafood in tomato sauce punched up with kimchi and fish sauce, like a Korean cioppino.</p><p>Tomato passata is essentially tomato puree. If you're shopping for canned tomato products and see a 24-ounce jar of tomato passata, that's perfect. I prefer it over chunky canned tomatoes for this recipe because the silky-smooth tomato texture is better for coating the seafood. If all you have is canned tomatoes, puree them in the blender first.</p><p>The specific seafood is less important than using the highest quality you can find. If the best thing in your area is clams and shrimp, and scallops are insanely expensive, go with those two and use more of them to make up the difference. Or use calamari or pieces of white fish fillets in place of the scallops, adding them at the end so they don't overcook. I love serving this with torn pieces of crusty bread for dipping directly into the pot, though I have also served it happily with pasta or rice.</p><h3>Kimchi Seafood Pot</h3><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Seafood</b><br>2 pounds mussels<br>1 pound cockles (or clams) or more mussels<br>All-purpose flour<br>Kosher salt<br>8 ounces jumbo or large shrimp (about 8)<br>8 ounces bay or sea scallops</p><p><b>Sauce</b><br>Vegetable oil<br>½ cup finely diced carrot<br>½ cup finely diced shallots<br>½ cup finely diced celery<br>1½ tablespoons minced garlic<br>2 scallions, white and green parts separated and thinly sliced crosswise<br>¼ cup chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, plus more for garnish<br>1 teaspoon kosher salt<br>½ cup chopped kimchi<br>1 tablespoon gochujang<br>½ cup white wine<br>3 cups (24 ounces) tomato passata (see headnote)<br>1 tablespoon fish sauce<br>½ teaspoon red pepper flakes</p><p><b>To serve</b><br>1 lemon<br>1 loaf good crusty bread</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Prep the seafood: If attached, pull the beards (the hairy bits near the joint) off the mussels. Scrub each well and drain, discarding any mussels that aren't firmly closed. Put the mussels in a bowl, cover with a cool, damp kitchen towel and refrigerate.</p><p>Put the cockles in a bowl with a pinch of flour and pinch of salt. Cover with cold water and let sit for 10 to 15 minutes while preparing the rest of the seafood. Drain the cockles, discarding any sand and grit at the bottom of the bowl and discard any that aren't firmly closed. Cover the bowl with a cool, damp kitchen towel and refrigerate.</p><p>For each shrimp, cut along the backbone and devein, leaving the shell and tails attached (though if you don't like peeling shrimp as you eat, remove the shell). For each scallop, peel off the small piece of muscle, if attached. If using scallops that are very large (like some sea scallops), halve them first so they cook evenly in the center at the same time as the shrimp.</p><p>Make the sauce: Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Add the carrot, shallots, and celery and cook, lowering the heat to medium if needed to prevent scorching and stirring often, until the shallots begin to soften, 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in the garlic, scallion whites, and parsley and cook until very fragrant, about 1 more minute. Stir in the salt and kimchi and cook until the kimchi begins to soften, about 2 minutes.</p><p>Stir in the gochujang, ensuring it is evenly dispersed, then pour in the wine. Increase the heat to medium-high and let the wine reduce by half. Stir in the tomato passata, fish sauce and red pepper flakes.</p><p>Cook the seafood: Stir the mussels and cockles into the pot and bring to a simmer. Cover and cook until the mussels and cockles have opened up, about 5 minutes; discard any that have not opened up. Stir in the shrimp and scallops, then cook uncovered, stirring often, until the rest of the seafood is cooked through, 2 to 3 minutes longer.</p><p>To serve: Using a Microplane rasp, grate the zest of the lemon into the pot. Cut the lemon in half and squeeze the juice from one half into the pot. Stir, then taste and add more lemon juice if you want. Garnish with the scallion greens and some parsley and serve immediately with crusty bread. This recipe is best as soon as it's made.</p><p><i>Esther Choi is a chef, entrepreneur and TV personality. She is the author of “Hand Taste: Cook Like a Korean Grandmother” and owner of Mokbar (with locations ranging from New York City to Las Vegas) and Ms. Yoo, a Korean-style gastropub in Manhattan. Choi is the co-host of the Food Network's “24 in 24” and the host of “Heat Eaters,” by “First We Feast.” Choi has been a finalist on “Iron Chef: Quest for an Iron Legend.” She lives in New York City with her husband and son.</i></p><p><i>Excerpted from “Hand Taste"”by Esther Choi. Copyright 2026 by Esther Choi. Used with permission of Voracious, an imprint of Little, Brown and Company, New York, NY. All rights reserved.</i></p>
