entries.title: Blackhawks could face reckoning next week if brutal road trip goes badly
entries.summary: <p>Russian rookie Roman Kantserov felt tired as he walked into the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' locker room Monday morning.</p><p>He's noticing a difference between the NHL's 84-game schedule and the KHL's 68-game schedule, even though — as he rides a five-game point streak — it doesn't seem to be affecting his performance.</p><p>"It's busy schedule. [It's] so hard," Kantserov said. "After Colorado, three games [to] play and then we have one week for rest, to take a breath."</p><p>Indeed, that four-day break between games next week should give the young Hawks a valuable opportunity to rejuvenate after grinding through nine games in 16 days.</p><p>But for Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson, that break could be the opposite of relaxing.</p><p>If Davidson is going to make any big changes to this struggling team — be it to Jeff Blashill's coaching staff or to the roster — things are aligning to make that break potentially the most logical time to do so.</p><p>Already, this season feels like it's reaching a boiling point. The Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/02/blackhawks-avalanche-patrick-kane-oliver-moore" >loss</a> Monday against the Avalanche worsened their record to 4-10-1, the second-worst in the NHL. Their negative-25 goal differential is tied for last, and their negative-110 shot-on-goal differential ranks second-last.</p><p>They're miles off pace from expectations, whether that's making the playoffs outright — which the players set as their goal — or hanging around the playoff bubble "deeper through the season, if not all the way through the season," as Davidson stated before training camp.</p><p>The Athletic and HockeyStats.com's projection models both give the Hawks a less than 1% chance of making the playoffs and forecast them to finish with 66 points, which would actually represent a six-point <i>drop</i> from last season.</p><p>A portion of the Hawks' fan base has been rioting on social media for weeks now, calling for everything short of dropping a bomb on the United Center.</p><p>Fans are always dramatic, and the most dramatic tend to be the loudest. They're ultimately the foundation of the organization, though, and they've clearly run out of patience. During the final minutes Monday, a handful tried to start a "fire Blashill" chant amid plentiful empty seats.</p><p>Inside the room, players seem to be handling this poor start admirably well. But as Connor Bedard said Monday, "I'd be lying if I said there's no frustration."</p><p>How much longer will Davidson stand by idly as temperatures continue to increase? </p><p>In theory, he could stand by for a while. He has proven to be a patient man, and he just received a major vote of confidence from chairman Danny Wirtz in April in the form of a contract extension.</p><p>Surely, though, urgency will compel action at some point. Davidson said before the opener that he anticipated ups and downs this season, but the fact there have been only downs and zero ups so far must be raising alarm bells.</p><p>The Hawks' challenging road trip this week presents one last opportunity for an upturn before the potential reckoning.</p><p>Without injured stars Patrick Kane and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/02/blackhawks-bowen-byram-injury-timeline-specialist" >Bowen Byram</a>, they'll face three of the league's best teams: the Panthers, Lightning and Hurricanes. They'll be heavy underdogs in each matchup, although it's worth noting they did win in both Tampa and Raleigh last season.</p><p>If the Hawks somehow escape this trip with multiple victories, they might buy themselves more time. If they return home with a record like 4-13-1, however, Davidson might be forced into action.</p><p>Could he really fire Blashill this soon? Could he fire one or more assistants but keep Blashill? Could he shake up the young core with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/01/blackhawks-trade-rumors-ivan-miroshnichenko-jake-debrusk-owen-tippett" >major trade</a>? Anything seems possible.</p><p>With two or three practices on the docket preceding the Sabres' visit next Thursday (Nov. 12), any newly brought-in coaches or players would have some time to alter the Hawks' systems or acclimate to the current ones before the schedule ramps up again.</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Bills release former Bears CB C.J. Gardner-Johnson
entries.summary: <p>The Bills released former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears </a>cornerback C.J. Gardner-Johnson on Tuesday after he served a one-game suspension for spitting toward Raiders tight end Brock Bowers.</p><p>Before then, Gardner-Johnson had started all six games for the Bills.</p><p>The Bears signed him last year with their defensive backfield depleted by injuries to Kyler Gordon, Jaylon Johnson and others. They chose not to re-sign him this offseason. While this year’s team has witnessed injuries to safety Coby Bryant and cornerback Malik Muhammad — the former is out until at least December and the latter missed Monday’s game — the Bears aren’t squeezed for depth quite as much as last year.</p><p>Kyler Gordon is the team’s slot cornerback —the place Gardner-Johnson played last year — and is one of its best defenders. Gardner-Johnson played safety in Buffalo, where Pro Football Focus graded him 71st out of 98 safeties.</p><p>Since 2023, he’s played the Lions, Eagles, Texans, Bears and Bills. He was drafted by the Saints, where he played for current Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen — and once goaded two different Bears players into ejections in the same season.</p><p>In 10 games for the Bears last year, he had two interceptions and three sacks.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: How Bears QB Caleb Williams mastered 'elaborate gameplan' vs. Seahawks
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Quarterback Caleb Williams reveled what felt like the most impactful win of the Ben Johnson era Monday night by looking into a swath of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> fans at Lumen Field screaming his name. When he was drafted by the Bears, he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/bears-seahawks-34-17-final-score-caleb-williams-i-want-to-make-these-fans-extremely-proud" >said to ESPN’s Scott Van Pelt, </a>he was told that Chicago was always a Bears town, even when Michael Jordan was winning titles. He believed it now, sitting on a studio set more than 2,000 miles away from Halas Hall.</p><p>In the hours that followed, the rest of America started acting like that group of navy-clad fans. Williams had 22-1 odds to win the league’s MVP award entering the weekend. He was down to 6-1 by Monday morning, behind only the Bills’ Josh Allen, the 49ers’ Brock Purdy and the Bengals’ Joe Burrow.</p><p>Williams — and the Bears — are having a moment.</p><p>What’s remarkable is what it took to get there Monday night. Williams didn’t have any jump passes in the 34-17 win against the Seahawks, and he certainly didn’t have to rally the Bears for a last-second win. Rather, Williams willed the Bears’ offense to success with efficiency. He checked into better plays at the line of scrimmage even with the Seahawks’ faithful at full throat. He made his throws on time. He made few mistakes, becoming just the 14<sup>th</sup> quarterback all season to throw at least 34 times in a game, get sacked only once and not intercepted at all.</p><p>Given the degree of difficulty — the Seahawks had the league's best defense before Monday — he was remarkable.</p><p>“This was one of the more elaborate game plans in terms of what we were asking him to do …” coach Ben Johnson said. “That had a lot to do with their scheme. And we needed that out of him to make sure we were getting into a good play that had a chance.”</p><p>Even when he made a mistake, he found a way to fix it. Up by three, the Bears faced third-and-four at the Seahawks’ 39 with about nine minutes to play. In the din of a crowd sensing a turning point, Williams took a delay of game. The Bears approached the line of scrimmage to run their next play on third-and-nine but were confused. Williams had missed a word in his play call.</p><p>“The crowd was loud at that point and I missed a word, one word or so,” Williams said.</p><p>When officials stopped the game to confer with Seahawks Mike Macdonald about whether he wanted to accept the penalty, Williams made sure the Bears lined up properly. He took the snap and threw a sidearm screen to Kalif Raymond, who danced upfield for 39 yards. The Bears scored one play later to seal the game.</p><p>That didn’t find its way onto Williams’ MVP ledger — it was technically a run play — but it mattered. So did the way he helped trick the Seahawks for the Bears’ first touchdown. After Roschon Johnson ran to the Seahawks’ 1 in the first quarter, the Bears went no-huddle, with Williams — and most of his teammates — giving hand signals as if they were going to run the same play again. Williams faked the handoff to Johnson, rolled right and threw a 1-yard touchdown to Luther Burden.</p><p>Both those plays take preparation.</p><p>“I want to be my best for Chicago, the organization, my teammates and things like that,” Williams said. “The more that I can do to be able to help this team, I'm going to spend extra time. Extra hours, extra walkthroughs, extra mental time to be able to have all the checks, have all the at-the-line stuff, these funky formations and all these different things to make it seem super complex for the defense …</p><p>“You put in all the work throughout the week to be able to have this feeling.”</p><p>Monday night, the Bears’ fans surrounding Williams could feel it. So could the rest of the country.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: 'El Jefe' takes charge: DT Jeffery Simmons embraces role, responsibility as new boss of Bears' defense
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> players couldn’t stop talking about defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons after his dominant debut Monday in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-big-plan-coming-together-beautifully-as-34-17-win-over-seahawks-pushes-them-to-best-start-since-2012" >their 34-17 win over the Seahawks</a>.</p><p>Offense or defense, it didn’t matter. Everyone had something to say.</p><p>They were happy when he arrived by trade from the Titans last week, but ecstatic once they saw the impact of one of the NFL’s best defenders blasting into the backfield in a No. 99 Bears jersey.</p><p>Quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> calls him, “Jefe,” the Spanish word for boss.</p><p>Fellow defensive tackle Grady Jarrett couldn’t wait to get a look at the game film for a better view of how Simmons loosened up the line of scrimmage for him, Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, James Lynch and other defensive linemen.</p><p>Cornerback Jaylon Johnson answered questions mostly by smiling.</p><p>Simmons embraced all of it, including the responsibility of being the new leader of this defense.</p><p>“You could feel the love,” Simmons said. “Around the building, everyone was excited.</p><p>“But they’re not going to be excited if I’m not out there doing my job. I know what comes with this job. ... If I’m not doing what I need to do to help this team win, I expect them to hold me to a high standard. It’s a two-way street.”</p><p>Rarely in recent Bears history has a trade looked so good so early. Just days into his team with the team, Simmons is a perfect fit.</p><p>Not that general manager Ryan Poles needed it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/31/jeffery-simmons-trade-bears-gm-ryan-poles-pursues-legendary-stuff-as-super-bowl-chase-officially-begins" >after feeling confident enough to trade two first-round picks to the Titans for him last week</a>, but he got instant confirmation that it was the right move.</p><p>Simmons and the Bears got everything they wanted out of the deal. The team added a much-needed force at the heart of its defense, and Simmons jumped from a plummeting Titans team to the center of a Super Bowl chase.</p><p>His excellence is no longer being wasted in obscurity. All those great plays carry a lot more importance here.</p><p>“The last couple years have been hard, not winning football games, but also, for me, it was like, ‘What can I do to help this team get back to that?” Simmons said. “It sucks that I wasn’t able to do that, but I’m a Chicago Bear now. Things change, and right now for me, to be able to be here, praise God.”</p><p>He led the team with six tackles, including a first-quarter sack and another tackle for loss, and was instrumental in a stellar game by Sweat and Lynch’s game-sealing interception. His impact rippled through the defense in subtle ways, too, as the Bears held the defending champions to one of their worst offensive games of the season.</p><p>That earned him a game ball from coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-coach-ben-johnson-is-not-here-merely-to-win-we-want-to-be-feared" >Ben Johnson</a> who yelled, “Welcome to the Bears, Jeffery Simmons,” as he handed it to him. Simmons replied enthusiastically, “I’m so happy to be a [expletive] Chicago Bear.”</p><p>The Seahawks would’ve preferred Poles wait another week before making the trade.</p><p>Running backs Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet combined for 49 yards on 16 carries. Quarterback Sam Darnold managed just 188 yards on 17-for-34 passing — his lowest completion percentage this season or last — with two touchdowns and an interception for a 74.1 passer rating.</p><p>The Bears have been calling Simmons as a “multiplier” because they expect he’ll make everyone around him better, and while that’s an overused term in the NFL, it certainly applies here.</p><p>Simmons’ effect on the defensive line is undeniable.</p><p>The Seahawks doubled him with center Jalen Sundell and guard Grey Zabel on Sweat’s sack in the third quarter — he had two others negated by penalties in the secondary — and left Sweat a very winnable one-on-one matchup against right tackle Abraham Lucas. He ripped past Lucas into a wide-open lane for the sack.</p><p>With the Seahawks desperately trying to rally late, Simmons and Sweat forced Darnold out of the pocket and into the face of Booker, who deflected his pass to Lynch for a pick that squashed the threat.</p><p>He also picked up two, maybe two and a half, linemen as Booker, immediately to the right of him, ran through to block Jason Meyers’ 33-yard field goal that would’ve pulled the Seahawks within a touchdown early in the fourth quarter.</p><p>But Simmons changed the game for the secondary, too.</p><p>“You know the ball has to come out,” Jaylon Johnson said. “It’s a lot easier to cover for two seconds than four, so you can be a little more aggressive.”</p><p>At one point on the sideline, Simmons exclaimed, “We don’t need to blitz!” because the Bears were getting consistent pressure from the defensive linemen. That’s a game-changer for defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, who had been running the fourth-most blitz-happy team in the league before Monday.</p><p>“That makes those guys’ job on the back end so much easier,” Simmons said.</p><p>He was conspicuous in every way, especially as the only Bears player wearing an undershirt with bright orange sleeves. He does that so his 3-year-old daughter can easily find him on TV — he wore red ones as a Titan — and it also was a helpful viewing enhancement for Bears fans wanting to zero in on the city’s newest sports star.</p><p>Sleeves or not, you couldn’t miss him. Individually, he was as advertised, and beyond that, he revolutionized the way the Bears played defense. For a team adamant that it’s ready to contend a championship, he sure looks like he was the missing piece.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Man, 26, shot in Humboldt Park dies
entries.summary: <p>A 26-year-old man shot in the Humboldt Park neighborhood has died, officials announced Tuesday. </p><p>Ricardo T. Bryant, 26, was shot Monday about 10:45 a.m. in the 3100 block of West Ohio Street, police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Bryant was sitting in a parked vehicle when he was shot by an assailant he did not know, police said. </p><p>Bryant was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, initially in critical condition but he died at 2:12 p.m. Monday, according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>An autopsy Tuesday determined Bryant, of the North Lawndale neighborhood, died of multiple gunshot wounds and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating. </p>
